title: Rollers capture first wheelchair basketball world title in 12 years
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia has defeated Italy 81-57 to win the men's IWBF World Championships final in Canada, giving the Rollers their third title in the tournament's history.

The result capped an unbeaten campaign for the Rollers in Ottawa, with the Australians proving again they are a giant of international wheelchair basketball by adding to their previous triumphs in 2010 and 2014.

Jaylen Brown played a starring role, scoring a game-high 28 points.

Captain Tom O'Neill-Thorne made a significant contribution on the scoreboard with a 20-point haul.

O'Neill-Thorne also managed 16 assists and seven rebounds in an outstanding all-around display.

Bill Latham provided valuable support with 12 points, seven rebounds and two assists.

The Rollers had an answer to every challenge posed by the Italians. (IWBF)

Italy had entered the gold-medal game with an undefeated record.

But the Rollers were in command from the opening quarter and led at every break.

They dominated Italy with 29 assists to 19 and out-rebounded their opponents 35-25.

The Rollers' defensive intensity shone through as they forced 13 turnovers and only conceded nine of their own.

title: Coalition vows to cut $15 off tank of petrol when global prices spike
text:
The opposition is promising to cut fuel costs when global prices spike, saying the measure would slash about $15 off the average tank of petrol.

Under the policy announced today, the Coalition said it would halve the fuel excise when the global price of Brent crude oil averages $US100 a barrel over two weeks.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the initiative, called Fuel Price Shield, would be "fully funded" through the Coalition's policy of cutting back the tobacco excise.

"Fuel Price Shield is all about providing relief at the bowser when it really counts," Mr Taylor said in Canberra.

"When we see two weeks where the price has averaged over $[US]100 a barrel, which means we're getting up towards $3 a litre at the bowser, there will be relief for Australians under a Coalition government."

He said Australian motorists were feeling pain at the pump, amid a re-escalation of war in the Middle East pushing up the price of petrol.

"We want to see $15 off a tank of petrol, 27 cents a litre, and that's fully funded through our cut to the tobacco excise," Mr Taylor said.

Petrol prices have risen again amid a re-escalation of conflict in the Middle East. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

The Coalition's policy to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent would raise $8 billion, according to modelling from the Parliamentary Budget Office.

Coalition unveils plan to slash tobacco tax A future Coalition government would slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent, legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches, and bolster law enforcement to shut down the illicit trade.

Mr Taylor said the Coalition would also eliminate the 32-cent road user charge for heavy vehicles to take pressure off the cost of transporting goods.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers dismissed the opposition's fuel policy, saying it was "uncapped and unfunded".

He told News24's Sunday Agenda the policy had more to do with "polling numbers than petrol prices", suggesting the Coalition was under pressure from One Nation.

Economist Chris Richardson said most economists have consistently said cutting the fuel tax is a "bad band-aid" that worsens inflation.

"That's the thing about a fuel tax cut, it simply adds to the amount of money sloshing around Australia," he said.

"It may reduce your bowser bill, but that comes at the cost of higher prices for everything else.

" It's a dumb policy at the best of times, and particularly dumb right now. "

He said both sides have either enacted or proposed fuel tax cuts in recent years, and both "have slagged off the other side for doing it".

Government not considering future fuel excise cuts

The government implemented a cut to the fuel excise, the amount of tax the government collects on petrol, from April 1 until the end of July this year.

That saw the fuel excise cut from 52.6 cents a litre to 20.6 cents a litre, a discount of 32 cents.

The measure was extended until midnight on August 2, but a rate rise in the excise rate meant the discount was 16 cents a litre.

Mr Chalmers was asked if the government would ever consider another fuel excise cut.

"It's not something that we've been discussing or considering, but we've shown a willingness over time to respond to the economic conditions," he said.

Jim Chalmers dismissed the Coalition's fuel excise cuts policy. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Taylor said it was "incredibly disappointing" to see the treasurer rule out the measure.

The opposition leader said Australians were facing potential further interest rate rises and cost-of-living pressures.

The government has previously criticised the Coalition's planned cuts to the tobacco tax, which would see a 20-pack of cigarettes drop from between $40–$50 to about $16–$26.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said that policy was "a guarantee we will see smoking and vaping rates in this country increase" and "will lead to deaths".

title: Man fined for failing to tag 'flighty' pet deer with 'sharp antlers'
text:
An elderly Adelaide Hills man who repeatedly tried to place mandatory identification ear tags on his "pet" deer — including an attempt to tranquillise them — has been fined after failing to succeed at the task.

The Environment, Development and Resources Court of South Australia found the 81-year-old owner of the deer had attempted to tag the animals, but both he and one of his sons were injured in the process.

In a published judgment, Senior Judge Michael Durrant said the man had also tried tagging the deer after they had shed their antlers.

"I was told the deer are described as flighty animals possessing sharp antlers," he said.

"Assistance was sought from a person associated with Monarto Zoo to tranquillise the animals.

" I am told those attempts were unsuccessful because the animals could not safely be approached. "

The judgment noted the man, who acquired the deer after he retired, had "a strong attachment" to the 30 to 40 deer on his property and "regards them as pets".

The man pleaded guilty to one count of failing to comply with an action order issued under the Landscape South Australia Act, an offence which carries a maximum penalty of $25,000.

The man kept as many as 40 deer at his Adelaide Hills property. File image. (ABC News : Luke Bowden)

Under state law, domestic deer over the age of 12 months must be fitted with a permanent ear tag bearing an identification number linked to the deer keeper's property. The animals must also be tagged before being moved to another property.

Extra time allowed, but still no compliance

A Landscape Officer noted the untagged deer in April 2022, and issued a compliance order requiring the animals be tagged by the end of August 2022, Senior Judge Durrant said.

He said the man did not comply, despite being given multiple extensions of time to do so.

According to the judgment, the property had facilities for the handling of deer on his property, but they had been destroyed in a bushfire and were yet to be restored "to their former condition".

"Notwithstanding those extensions, the requirements of the action order remained unfulfilled," Senior Judge Durrant said.

"There are several practical difficulties associated with compliance with the order."

A judge convicted and fined the man. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Senior Judge Durrant said the man "was afforded several opportunities to comply with the action order" but the "circumstances do not suggest a deliberate refusal to engage with the regulatory process or an absence of effort directed toward compliance".

"The defendant nevertheless remained under an obligation to comply with the action order," he said.

" The practical difficulties he encountered do not excuse the offending. "

Senior Judge Durrant said the requirement to tag domestic deer served several purposes.

"The identification regime assists in the management of disease risk, biodiversity impacts, habitat degradation, wildfire management and conservation planning," he said.

He noted the man's advanced age, poor health, lack of prior offending, limited financial means and that he had otherwise been cooperative with authorities.

Senior Judge Durrant convicted the man and, after applying a discount for his guilty plea, fined the man $6,300.

He also ordered that all deer at the property over 12 months of age be fitted with a permanent ear tag by the end of November.

title: Tips for tackling jetlag when travelling with kids
text:
Anyone who has flown with or near children can picture it: the crying kid, the frazzled parent and the cranky passengers.

Travelling with children can be tough, and the difficulties can escalate when you cross a time zone or two.

Things don't necessarily improve when you touch down, either. After long-haul travel, jet lag can impact our health for days afterwards.

Most adults have experienced jet lag, but what about when children are involved?

What exactly is jet lag?

Jet lag refers to the temporary misalignment of a person's internal body clock (or circadian rhythm) with the local time where they are. In other words, the body is still operating according to the time zone it has just come from, rather than the new time zone.

As the name suggests, jet lag is generally caused by air travel when you cross multiple time zones very quickly before the body can adapt.

It can make you feel fatigued and sluggish during the day and make it hard to sleep at night in your new location.

Is it worse flying in a certain direction?

Yes, jet lag is worse when you travel east.

When travelling east, you are essentially "losing" time. This means when you try to go to bed at your destination, your body clock still thinks it is much earlier in the day.

You might find yourself lying awake at night because your body isn't ready for sleep yet. Or you might wake up at a time that feels like the middle of the night.

When travelling west, your body clock is essentially "behind" the local time. This means you may start to feel sleepy earlier than usual because your body thinks it is later than it really is.

Fortunately for people travelling west, it's generally easier to stay awake later than it is to fall asleep earlier. This means you can often push through some afternoon or early evening sleepiness until a more reasonable bedtime.

The good news is, you can start adjusting your or your child's body clock before you leave home. (Woman raising her hand on passenger seat, Steven Thompson, license)

How does jet lag affect kids?

Children tend to experience similar symptoms to adults, such as:

finding it hard to get to sleep or stay asleep

being cranky

not wanting to eat at mealtime

nausea

generally feeling fatigued.

Surprisingly, not a lot of research has been done comparing the effects of jet lag in children with jet lag in adults.

What we do know suggests children might actually be affected a little less than adults. This might be because children produce more melatonin, which could help them adjust to new time zones a little quicker. Melatonin is the "sleepiness hormone" that our body naturally produces.

Evidence also suggests that as we age, we become less tolerant of jet lag. However, most of this evidence has looked at comparisons of young adults and older adults, so may not necessarily reflect the differences between adults and children.

Tips to reduce jet lag before you fly

The good news is, you can start adjusting your or your child's body clock before you leave home.

This generally requires precise control of light exposure and possibly adjusting sleep times in the days before departure.

Every hour you shift before boarding is one less hour to catch up at the other end, though this means you are starting the jet lag early, at home.

Shifting the body clock before travel is demanding for anyone, but with children you are also managing someone else's schedule, energy and patience. Someone who might not understand why they need to sleep an hour earlier than usual.

For many families, this isn't realistic. However, from the moment you disembark, there's plenty you can do.

Tips once you land

Your most powerful jet lag tool is free: daylight.

As a general rule of thumb, being exposed to morning light shifts your body clock earlier. Light in the late afternoon or evening shifts your body clock later.

Officials intercept 150,000 melatonin units at border amid crackdown Australian Border Force officials have intercepted more than 150,000 units of melatonin in four months, after authorities warned they would crack down on unregulated products.

Getting this timing right at your destination is the single most effective thing you can do to combat jet lag for you and your child.

Habitual time cues (everyday things that signal the time to your body, such as mealtimes or bedtime routines) can also help with the shift to a new time zone.

Try to move mealtimes to local schedules as quickly as possible.

Where you can, keep bedtime routines consistent. A familiar sequence of bath, story and lights out carries more weight than most parents realise. For young children, routine is one of the strongest signals that sleep is coming, regardless of what the clock says.

What about tech or medication?

Most jet lag apps rely on the same principles: that light, melatonin and exercise can shift the body clock, and that timing matters.

If you are using an app or related technology, the amount of personalisation it includes is likely to determine how useful it is. At a minimum, apps should include questions about your sleep history, usual sleep schedule, chronotype (whether you are a morning or evening person) and travel itinerary.

Some people also use melatonin supplements for themselves, or their children, while travelling.

But unless you are working with a healthcare provider like a paediatrician, it's generally not recommended to use these supplements. Taking the wrong dose, or taking melatonin at the wrong time, can actually make jet lag worse, for both adults and kids.

Madeline Sprajcer is a senior lecturer in psychology and Dean J Miller is a sleep and circadian scientist, both at CQUniversity Australia. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: Meet the gig workers helping train robots to do our dishes
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Mohamad Dunggio recently strapped a mobile phone to his head and recorded himself doing his dishes over and over again for four hours.

It left him with wrinkly fingers, but he did not mind.

"I think it's OK because I exchange my time to earn money," said the 23-year-old from Gorontalo on Sulawesi in Indonesia.

Mr Dunggio is one of the thousands of gig workers around the world feeding the robotics industry's insatiable demand for training data.

Since April he has been earning extra cash making "egocentric training" videos, used to teach robots how to do things like household chores.

Egocentric training data is sensor or video recordings made from the perspective of the person doing the task, often captured with a head or chest-mounted camera with a focus on keeping the subject's hands in the frame.

One of the tasks Mohamad Dunngio was paid to do was cleaning his sink. (Supplied)

Mr Dunggio said he was paid by three companies from Argentina, India and the US between $US3 ($4.22) and $US10 an hour to record himself performing tasks like dishwashing, cleaning, cooking, making the bed, ironing, folding clothes and sweeping.

"I think it's a good thing to do because you don't have to have any experience," he said.

How to teach robots

As the recent World Humanoid Robot Games in China demonstrated, robots have been advancing in literal leaps and bounds in recent years.

But the dream of a multi-function humanoid robot that can move around the home efficiently and reliably taking on a variety of domestic tasks has so far proven elusive.

A Chinese company demonstrated a robot that does laundry last month at the World Robot Conference in Beijing. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

Dana Kulić, a robotics professor at Monash University, said that for robots to navigate the huge variety and complexity of people's homes they needed to learn how to observe and react to their environments.

"Even if the task is just to fold the laundry, or wash the dishes, every person has a different set of dishes. Then the place where [the clothes] should be folded looks different," she said.

The robot that can beat Usain Bolt A robot has beaten Usain Bolt's 100 metres world record.

Professor Kulić said robotics researchers were using egocentric data in a way similar to how generative AI researchers taught large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to predict the next word or letter in a sentence.

While egocentric data produced by actual robots, teleoperated by a human, tended to be more relevant, human egocentric data was cheaper, easier and could provide a much-needed variety of scenarios, she said.

The workers producing the data now include entire factories in South Asia, house cleaners in the US and home delivery drivers.

However, Professor Kulić said the ways human egocentric data was collected were not without issues.

They ranged from whether the contributors truly understood what the data was being used for to privacy concerns about filming in people's homes and data being sold on to third companies.

Strict requirements for videos

Mr Dunggio said overall he was happy with the side-hustle and did not feel exploited, even if others might feel differently.

"If people don't have work and are looking for income this is just an option," he said.

However, he said he felt a bit embarrassed going to the mall with a phone mounted on his head and was disappointed when some of his videos were rejected.

Appen produces egocentric videos accompanied by data collected via extra sensors. (Supplied)

He also complained that some companies charged a transfer fee of about $US1 to withdraw accumulated earnings of under $US10.

On the plus side he got to learn some new skills.

"I never cooked for myself before, but now I know how to cook," he said.

Changes in demand for data

Sergio Bruccoleri is vice-president of delivery for Appen, an ASX-listed Australian company that collects and annotates datasets for the tech industry, including egocentric data for robotics.

Mr Bruccoleri, who is based in Barcelona, said the company could collect around 60,000 hours of video per month from as many as 5,000 contributors all over the world, including India, Canada, the US, Brazil, Mexico and the Philippines.

China was Appen's biggest market for robotics data with the US second, he said.

He said Appen's contributors produced videos in homes and increasingly in workplaces but also in controlled studios, sometimes with specialised cameras and equipment like sensor gloves.

However, he said Appen was moving away from the kind of data that was being collected at an industrial scale in "lower-cost countries" because it had become commoditised and de-valued.

Sergio Bruccoleri says demand is increasing for egocentric data produced in wealthier countries. (Supplied)

The company was increasingly focused on wealthier countries like the US and Canada, where the robots were likely to be sold initially, while still gathering high value data elsewhere.

"The dishwashers in the US look very different from the dishwashers you would have elsewhere," he said.

In the past, Appen has faced criticism over pay and conditions. Contributors on forums still complain of issues from late payments to poor communication and unexplained account cancellations.

Mr Bruccoleri said some of Appen's systems were not perfect and the company tried to address contributor issues with open lines of communication.

He said Appen had a code of ethics and fair-pay standards and tried "as much as possible" to ensure pay was "always above the minimum wage set in that particular country".

'Ghost workers' speak out Artificial intelligence is built by an army of global workers who are speaking out about ill-treatment from data labelling companies.

Appen also had privacy guidelines for contributors and a tracing system which he said meant they should be able to request the data they produced be withdrawn, even after it had been sold.

Asked whether it was unfair that contributors were sometimes forced to pay fees to withdraw their earnings, Mr Bruccoleri said he believed it was but it was the payment platforms that took the fee.

"It's not limited to Appen. You see it in other platforms all the time," he said.

When can I have a robot to fold my clothes?

Robotics companies, particularly those in China, have this year been unveiling more and more competent humanoid models that appear close to the ideal of a Jetsons-style robot to do all our household chores.

But Professor Kulić believes that is still a way off.

She said there was a big difference between showing a robot folding clothes during a demonstration and having it working reliably for extended periods of time.

Then there was the cost, not only to produce the robots but also to maintain and repair them.

"I feel like there's many problems to be solved beyond just the ability to do a specific task," she said.

She compared robots to autonomous vehicles which worked "99 per cent of the time".

"But now that last 1 per cent is taking much more time than anyone initially thought it would," Professor Kulić said.

title: His Eliza statue is Insta famous, but boats are Tony's true passion
text:
Tell us about your experience.

His statue of Eliza in the Swan River has a cult following and its own social media pages, while another of CY O'Connor riding his horse in the ocean is a much-loved North Coogee landmark.

But Tony Jones's art is better defined by its strong maritime theme, which was inspired by sailing at Chidley Point on the Swan River from the time he was a boy.

"It just made sense to me. You sit down with a piece of paper, what am I going to draw? I'd better draw a boat," the 81-year-old said, laughing.

The statue of "Eliza" the swimmer in Crawley Bay is one of Jones's most recognisable works. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Boat parts are often incorporated into Jones's sculptures. He also uses sailing motifs and has re-imagined navigational markers as striking art pieces.

His sprawling workshop near Fremantle is a treasure trove of his passions.

Signals turned sculptures crowd the workshop. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

There are sculptures of birds, maritime markers and wind catchers, half-made projects and every sort of material for future projects, including decades-old wooden beams from long-dismantled jetties.

And there are, of course, boats. Everywhere.

Boats are everywhere in Jones's studio. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Slung from the roof, stacked against a wall, preserved under tarpaulins, and in the work bay, historic, often rare, wooden Swan River sailing dinghies that Jones has collected over the past 30 years.

"They remind us of the things we did, the precursors to the way things are now. And they're beautiful craft objects, too," he said.

One of the boats being restored. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Historic 'Sharpies'

Among the boats in the work bay are two "Sharpies" that legendary Western Australian sailor Rolly Tasker used in the lead up to, and during, the 1956 Melbourne Olympics.

The historic Falcon III won Australia its first sailing Olympic medal. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Tasker and Malcolm "Huck" Scott won silver, Australia's first ever Olympic sailing medal, at the event.

Matt Dickmann, Jones' long-time collaborator, sailor, artist and woodworker is restoring the Sharpies, known as Falcon 3 and Falcon 4.

Matt Dickmann is a long-time friend and collaborator who also loves boats. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

"I'm trying to finish it in a sense that everyone can appreciate what it used to look like," Dickmann said.

"One of the amazing stories about this boat is that this timber here is spruce and it was salvaged by Rolly from a plane that used to fly to Rottnest and back."

Jones and Dickmann share a love of boats and sailing. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

A place to call home

Jones's boat collection is so expansive, that he has teamed up with friends, neighbours, sailors and volunteers to set up the Swan River Sailing Dinghy Heritage Association which aims to restore the dinghies and find a permanent place for the collection.

"A bit of a men's shed for boating," he said.

The association wants the boats to be put on display, ideally in a traditional boat shed by the edge of the river, in partnership with a local government, yacht club or the WA Maritime Museum.

A lifetime of sailing has inspired Jones. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

The shed would be a place to preserve that history of sailing and boat-making on the Swan River, as well as a place to bring boat enthusiasts together.

Lotterywest provided a grant to restore Rolly Tasker's Sharpies, and would like to see them displayed.

"These boats were involved in the first Olympic sailing win, which was an amazing feat," Lotterywest's Nikki Wilson-Smith said.

"Making them available to the WA public is a really an important thing."

The collection of historic boats is awaiting a public home. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Tony Jones and his group of boat enthusiasts are still searching for that place.

title: Warning for brain health over offloading deep-thinking skills to AI
text:
Tell us about your experience.

With the widespread use of artificial intelligence in schools and universities, there are concerns about its impact on learning and ultimately young brains.

"[AI] can be a great tool; it can help stimulate critical thinking, for example, if used in the right way," neuroscientist Professor James Vickers said.

But he said a recent study of students in China highlighted problems with offloading hard mental work to AI.

Published this year, the study of more than 26,000 students in grades 7 to 12 looked at how generative AI affected homework productivity and learning.

It found AI use lifted homework scores by 18 per cent and improved completion times by 30 per cent.

But it lowered monthly exam scores by 20 per cent within six months.

Professor Vickers has concerns that using AI instead of developing deep-thinking skills could have long-term impacts. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

"There is a risk with AI that it is really going to be affecting our brain function into our future lives," Professor Vickers said.

AI and brain plasticity

Learning and deep thinking physically alter the human brain, creating new connections between neurons.

It is known as brain plasticity.

"The brain almost quadruples in weight from birth to adulthood, without adding any new neurons — it's all physical change driven by learning," University of Tasmania senior neuroscience lecturer Dr Matt Kirkcaldie said.

Neuroscientists are looking into the impact of offloading deep thinking to AI. (Jon Olav Eikenes / FlickrCC)

Over time, critical thinking, learning, and other cognitive tasks help build robust nerve networks that underlie what is known as cognitive reserve.

"[Cognitive reserve] is your ability to resist things that negatively impact the brain, that might be stroke or brain injury, multiple sclerosis and even dementia," Professor Vickers said.

Cognitive reserve is built up from early life through schooling, then higher education.

There are concerns AI could impair the development of critical thinking skills.

"They might read the AI-generated text and understand what it says, but they never went through the struggle of working through the ideas and how they might fit in the overall picture," Dr Kirkcaldie said.

A recent report by the eSafety Commission found 78 per cent of Australian children had used an AI assistant.

Professor Vickers has concerns that using AI instead of developing deep-thinking skills could have long-term impacts.

" The theory is that if you don't build up that kind of connectivity, then when you are impacted by a brain disease such as dementia then the chances are you will develop it earlier than not. "

The young people boycotting AI

Alexis Shegog and her friends refuse to use artificial intelligence. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Some young people are so worried about the impact artificial intelligence could have on their learning they have decided to boycott it.

"I wouldn't want to cheapen my experience at uni, especially with the fees we pay," said Alexis Shegog, who is planning to return to university.

Alexis is part of a group called circa Lutruwita, which has been protesting the development of AI data centres in northern Tasmania.

Alexis Shegog and fellow members of the group circa Lutruwita protest against proposals for data centres in Tasmania and the impact of AI in general. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The group has concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centres and its use in military settings.

They are also worried about AI deepfakes and their impact on personal privacy.

And while they refuse to use AI as part of their studies, they are aware that AI will be in their futures.

"I would want to make sure that I was getting the full value from my course and learning the material, especially if I'm going to have to compete with AI in the future for my job," Ms Shegog said.

Members of circa Lutruwita making posters. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

"My friends who are in uni at the moment, none of them use AI.

"And most of them are quite concerned about the impact that it has environmentally, socially, and the impact that it is having on their education."

Students not using AI are the exception

A recent report by the eSafety Commission found 78 per cent of Australian children had used an AI assistant.

Ninety-one per cent used it for learning or translation, 70 per cent used it for writing or editing, and 68 per cent used it for entertainment.

Students at Guilford Young College in Hobart have mixed feelings about the technology.

Lacey Tilyard says she uses AI for some subjects but not others. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Some said they used it for creating practice tests or simplifying ideas.

"I used it a lot last year for my science-based subjects to explain the more complex topics," Lacey Tilyard said.

But she said some of her classes, like psychology, have a strict ban on the use of AI.

Ella Willmott said AI was a good learning tool and had helped her research future employment opportunities.

Ella Willmott has mixed feelings about the technology. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

But she was worried about its impact on creativity.

"I think it's the worst thing for artists. Because it just gets rid of the authenticity and almost the rawness of everyone's art," she said.

How should AI in education be managed?

Professor Vickers said AI may drive a transformation in how educators teach and how student learning is assessed.

"It may be possible to adapt AI engines to encourage critical thinking and learning, so that the AI enables learning rather than replacing it," he said.

Professor Kathy Mills, from the Institute for Learning Sciences and Teacher Education at the Australian Catholic University, said teachers want their students to use AI critically.

"Both students and teachers want AI tools that are designed to do more than tell the answers, but which guide student learning," she said.

She said how student learning was assessed would be more important than ever.

Kathy Mills says teachers want their students to use AI critically. (Supplied)

"If teachers want to know what students can do without AI, take-home assignments are going to be more difficult for teachers to monitor the level of AI support accessed by students in that context," she said.

Professor Vickers said rethinking education was not just about "trying to catch students out" through exams.

But he said it was about ensuring students could apply learning to different situations, in the same way medical students were presented with clinical scenarios to test their knowledge.

title: Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools
text:
Tell us about your experience.

In Victoria's tropical north, where the Murray River winds, a select group of houses are selling for half of what you'd expect.

It's got nothing to do with changes in the housing market and can trip up even the most savvy investor.

The unusual house prices are thanks to the 140-year-old legacy of two Canadian engineers who decided education should be the benefactor of their entrepreneurial endeavours.

Mildura's founders set aside one-fifteenth of the town's available land to generate funds for education in the region. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Mildura's college lease scheme is unique.

No other Australian town has one.

In the citrus capital, 184 lots are leased to individuals and organisations instead of being sold freehold.

Basically, someone can own the improvements but not the land itself.

Officially, the land is owned by the Victorian education minister.

Revenue from the lease agreements goes directly to schools in Sunraysia, which use the funds to buy new classroom equipment and technology that they would otherwise go without.

A Department of Education spokesperson said the Mildura Schools Land Trust disburses about $1.95 million annually to 27 primary and secondary schools, providing additional funding that benefits more than 9,000 students.

Canadian engineers William B Chaffey and George Chaffey founded the township of Mildura. (Supplied: Chaffey Trail)

A lofty deal

In 1886, the Victorian government signed a deal with Canadian engineers George and William Chaffey to build the Mildura irrigation settlement.

Historian and former primary school principal Bob Walton said the Chaffey brothers set aside one-fifteenth of available land to generate funds for an agricultural college, although this was never built.

Instead, a local high school became the first to benefit from the lease funds.

"They decided to set aside and not sell some of the allotments in the colony," he said.

"The Chaffeys were very interested in education."

Mr Walton said the Chaffey brothers were inspired by a similar scheme in California, their base before coming to Australia.

'Cheap' prices grab buyer attention

College lease properties often appear in real estate listings for what, at first glance, seem like a bargain price.

One home recently sold for a reported $300,000 on Mildura's Lemon Avenue where, across the road, a similar freehold property fetched almost $550,000 two months earlier.

"Obviously, there's lease land for other things, but not like this. This is very unique," Ray White Mildura managing director Damian Portaro said.

"It's interesting having to explain to a buyer from Melbourne or Sydney exactly what this is.

" It's 100 years old now, this system. It was probably ahead of its time back then, but I haven't seen it or heard of it anywhere else. "

Agent Damian Portaro says investors are drawn to college lease homes. (Supplied: Ray White Real Estate)

Mr Portaro said the property listings appealed to first home buyers, but they often ran into difficulty obtaining finance due to the unusual lease clause.

He said most buyers of college lease land were investors rather than owner-occupiers.

"They might get in for half the price, for example, then they start factoring in 'there's rates, there's insurances, there's a college lease I have to pay.'"

Unlocking housing supply

Mallee Accommodation and Support Program (MASP) has utilised the scheme to build social housing on five college-lease properties with assistance from Homes Victoria.

Charmaine Calis is the CEO of MASP, which has built social housing on five college lease properties. (Supplied: MASP)

"We see it as a really good way to have two social goods out of the one block of land — both continuing to support local schools and also building social and affordable housing onto it," chief executive Charmaine Calis said.

MASP told a parliamentary inquiry last year the Victorian government should look at more ways college leases could ease the housing crisis.

"We do need to increase the supply of housing available, and this is certainly one way we can look at doing that," Ms Calis said.

title: Emergency helicopters still unable to land at two SA regional hospitals
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Emergency helicopters remain unable to use the helipad at the regional hospitals in Victor Harbor and Murray Bridge.

South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer said the issues at Murray Bridge were close to being resolved, but the situation at Victor Harbor was "complex" and would need a long-term solution.

The Victor Harbor Childcare and Education Centre sits alongside the helipad. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The sites are the final two to reopen after 13 regional helipads were temporarily closed in 2024 because they did not meet new Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) guidelines.

The helipads cannot be used until certified as safe by Babcock, the current operators of the MedSTAR helicopter service.

Issues remain around the required downwash exclusion zone and the proximity of houses at Murray Bridge, and a community-run childcare centre at Victor Harbor.

The centre has a peppercorn lease in place with SA Health until 2030.

The childcare centre is adjacent to the helipad. (Supplied: David Basham)

Mr Boyer told state parliament last month there had been discussions with residents of Murray Bridge who "might be in a home that is in the downwash area" and that he "hoped to have positive news soon".

However, he said reinstating the Southern Fleurieu Health Service's helipad at Victor Harbor would take "longer-term planning".

Independent member for Finniss Lou Nicholson said it was her understanding the minister was trying to find a solution ahead of the lease expiry date.

Lou Nicholson is the independent member for Finniss. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

From her conversations with government, she said she understood that it was not the government's intention to wait until the lease expired.

"If indeed the path ahead is finding a new location for the childcare centre, that work does need to be underway now," she said.

A community and education centre is located adjacent to the helipad in Victor Harbor. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Hor)

One Nation member for Hammond Robert Roylance raised the Murray Bridge helipad in parliament last month.

While happy with indications it was closer to opening, he said his electorate wanted a clearer response.

"Can we expect it in three months, six months? Soon is good, but what is soon?" he said.

Robert Roylance says his electorate needs to know when the helipad will be operational. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Roylance said a 66-metre space was required around the helicopter landing site and he understood several houses were within that area.

In a statement provided to the ABC, Mr Boyer said $23.4 million had been invested to upgrade regional helipads across the state to meet updated CASA requirements, and work continued to bring the two remaining sites back into operation.

"Medical retrieval services remain available for the community and surrounding areas by utilising alternative sites nearby.

"Patient, staff and community safety remain the priority."

title: In an outback town, this small venue raised $1 million to save itself
text:
Tell us about your experience.

It might seem unlikely that a volunteer-run venue in one of the country's most remote towns could inspire people from across Australia and the world to help raise $1 million to save it.

But it did.

Over the past month, the founders of popular Alice Springs live music venue The Black Wreath have been fundraising to buy the building and turn the whole block into a creative hub after their landlord put the property up for sale.

Artists and music industry figures came on board, including Amyl and the Sniffers, who played at The Black Wreath's Blacken Open Air festival in 2022, as well as donors who matched pledges dollar for dollar.

Loading Instagram content

The Black Wreath hosts local gigs and offers artists a recording and rehearsal space, helping kick-start the careers of some of the most remote bands in the world.

Before he launched the campaign on August 4, the Black Wreath's founder, who goes by the mononym Pirate, hardly used social media.

But by the end of the appeal, he was posting daily videos, pushing as hard as he could to save one of the creative heartbeats of Alice Springs.

"It's a massive milestone, I'm really proud of the community achievement and everyone that's gotten behind this," he said.

The fundraisers gave themselves until September 13 to reach their $1 million funding goal, but hit the target two days early before a massive weekend of coordinated gigs across the country in solidarity with the cause.

Pirate says he hopes to run The Black Wreath as a foundation. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

It wasn't until the day after the Alice Springs gig, headlined by South East Desert Metal, that Pirate had his first day off in months.

He said the whole town "became a metal head for the night".

"The last month it's been 12 to 15 hours every single day, it hasn't been healthy, but it's been necessary," Pirate said.

" And yesterday I just absolutely collapsed, couldn't do a bloody thing. "

However, Pirate said there was a long road still ahead.

As part of the fundraising campaign, people from across the country made pledges for something in return, which ranged from T-shirts, records, rings and hats to an entire festival, Blacken Open Air, to be held on April 30 next year.

"I'm not celebrating yet just yet; I'm getting back to work," Pirate said.

Loading...

"It's just the beginning of the process, we've raised some money and now we need to negotiate with the owners.

"There's a lot more to do."

Pirate said the grand vision was to turn the entire property into a creative precinct.

"My big hopes and aspirations and dreams are that it's run as a foundation and the income generated goes into local music and arts," he said.

"And touring Central Australian artists outside of here, [as well as] bringing artists to Alice Springs and putting them on stages here as well.

"Fifteen years of doing this, I find that the travel aspect has been the biggest hindrance to connecting us with a wider community."

Ltyentye Apurta/Santa Teresa musicians South East Desert Metal describe themselves as the most isolated touring band in the world, and credit The Black Wreath for success that's seen them perform on the steps of the Sydney Opera House.

The band's lead vocalist and guitarist, Chris Wallace, said there was nothing else like it in Alice Springs.

The fundraiser to save The Black Wreath has been hailed as "an amazing moment for the whole nation". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I really love it, all that comes from Black Wreath," he said.

" Black Wreath was the one that found us, and made us who we are. "

Reflecting on the successful fundraiser, Pirate said it was "an amazing moment for the whole nation, especially for the heavy metal community".

"This is very historic," he said.

"I'm proud to be a part of that community and we're as far away from everyone as you can possibly get, but right now it feels like there's no distance at all between us."

title: John Farnham to miss tribute concert due to poor health
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed ahead of the Melbourne event.

The concert, dubbed The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend, will be held at Rod Laver Arena this evening, with funds raised on the night going towards the cancer service that supported Farnham during his cancer battle.

In a statement posted on social media, Farnham's wife, Jill, and sons, Robert and James, wrote that the singer was "deeply moved" by the musical tribute but would be too unwell to attend the arena spectacular.

John Farnham performing his 1986 smash hit You're the Voice at a 2017 charity concert. (ABC News: Kristian Silva)

His family confirmed the 77-year-old You're the Voice singer required continuous oxygen support and was receiving 24-hour nursing care.

"Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending tomorrow night to watch it all happen," the Farnham family statement said.

"Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John's health to help explain why.

"John's health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility.

"It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it."

Farnham's 1986 comeback, Whispering Jack, was one of Australia's best-selling albums and relaunched the singer's career. (ABC)

Some of the biggest names in Australian entertainment are scheduled to take centre stage at the Farnham tribute tonight, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson.

International stars, including Canadian singer Celine Dion and American crooner Richard Marx, are also taking part in the event, which will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia.

"We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John's changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John's fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend," the Farnham family said.

"If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person.

" As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable. "

John Farnham is one of Australia's most successful performers. (ABC TV)

Australian pop band Human Nature, who featured in John Farnham's song Every Time You Cry, said they "can't wait" to celebrate the 77-year-old's career at tonight's concert.

"This weekend, we celebrate the extraordinary music and legacy of the one and only John Farnham — a true living legend and a hero to us all," the band said in a social media post.

"It's impossible not to feel emotional, and incredibly humbled, to have played even a small part in John's remarkable career.

"John, we love you. Thank you for welcoming us into your world."

The original yellow Wiggle, Greg Page, said in a social media post: "All our love and understanding is being sent to John and his family".

Farnham is one of Australia's most successful performers, with his 1986 album, Whispering Jack, selling more than 1.6 million copies.

The British-born singer was named 1987 Australian of the Year by then-prime minister Bob Hawke, and has won more than 20 ARIA awards.

In 2024 Farnham released an autobiography, The Voice Inside, which details the monumental triumphs of his career as well as the immense struggles he has faced.

title: 'We are really scared': NDIS provider shutters day program as federal cuts loom
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Canberra community members are concerned that the closure of a local NDIS program does not bode well for the disability community ahead of looming federal cuts to the scheme.

Carers ACT will close its hub disability day program and NDIS support coordination service at the start of October, citing operating costs and funding arrangements, with advocates worried it may not be the last.

The NDIS overhaul will result in many being kicked off or prevented from accessing the now-$50 billion scheme, and being moved to yet-to-be-built state- and territory-run supports.

The overhaul is expected to save an estimated $37.8 billion over the next four years.

The Carers ACT hub program aimed to help with independent living skills and daily activities including household chores, music and social outings.

Powerful testimonies heard at NDIS inquiry The key takeaways from the six-day Senate inquiry into a proposed NDIS shake-up.

Benjamin Zarew, a disability advocate and NDIS recipient himself, said he attended the ACT Carers day program to improve his mental wellbeing and spend time out of the house.

"I feel sad, but there's opportunity with other agencies [for me]," he said.

"I'm worried about the other people who may not be aware because of their disabilities … some people have to have a constant routine, and that change is going to feel that effect."

The federal government's NDIS bill passed after a deal between Labor and the Coalition, but not without heavy criticism from the Greens and ACT senator David Pocock.

Mr Zarew said he was very "disappointed in the politicians for basically allowing this bill to go through".

Looming NDIS cuts instil fear in Canberrans NDIS recipient Nicci Carlson, who is in constant pain and may soon lose her eyesight, says cuts to the scheme are making vulnerable people living with a disability scapegoats for Australians hit hard by cost-of-living pressures.

The now-passed bill includes a detail that has been heavily criticised by those living with a disability, their advocates and others in the disability sector.

The NDIS minister of the day would be given powers to slash social and community participation funding for each NDIS recipient's plan by up to 50 per cent.

These cover things such as hiring support workers to take participants to the doctor or supermarket.

Mr Zarew faces that particular cut himself. His own plan is poised to be slashed as the changes come into effect.

Others have warned that their plans have already been cut, despite the changes not having come into full effect yet — they will be made official in October this year.

"It's going to limit what I can do; I'm a bit nervous about that," he said of the upcoming cuts.

"It's going to be challenging for everyone… I think it is going to be really harmful.

" They say they want disabled people in the community to be out, seen and heard, but we are going back to being ghosts essentially. "

Official concerns

In a statement posted to its website, Carers ACT said: "Like many organisations across the community sector, Carers ACT is responding to increasing operating costs, funding pressures and changes across the disability and aged care sectors".

"After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to close the Hub Disability Day Program and our NDIS Support Coordination services," the statement said.

"Changes to funding arrangements mean these services have increasingly required Carers ACT to subsidise their delivery, and this is no longer financially sustainable."

MLA Laura Nuttall says people are fearful over the looming NDIS cuts. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

ACT Greens MLA Laura Nuttall said the fear is rife in the community as the cuts loom, as "people don't know exactly what's coming".

"People are contacting our office all the time, saying, ' Hey, please fight this; we are really scared'," she said.

"And I don't blame them; their human rights are being put up for debate."

Ms Nuttall is concerned the local ACT government does not have a safety net for disability programs which will be affected by the cuts, as they begin to roll in.

"I think a lot of people in our community feel this is the sign of the times and that this is not the first or last program that we are going to see cut for people with a disability," she told the ABC.

" Where are these supports that are supposed to catch us? …I don't think the territory is prepared for it. "

Shannon Kolak, the CEO of Act Down Syndrome and Intellectual Disability, said the closure was devastating for the disabled community, as some had attended the hub five days a week for years, and she also wasn't sure how the ACT would shoulder more of the services.

She added that the closure of the Carers ACT NDIS support program was devastating as good support coordinators are hard to find.

"Day programs especially, or programs that rely on people's social and community participation [NDIS] funding may not be able to offer services anymore," she said.

Carers ACT has been contacted for comment.

title: Wallaroos collapse against France as bus fire delays game
text:
Australia's Wallaroos have been left frustrated by a potentially massive Test win that got away as undisciplined France somehow escaped with a 29-26 win after being 19 points down and reduced at one point to just 11 players.

On an extraordinary day of Test rugby, exacerbated by off-field drama when the second half had to be delayed due to a bus on fire adjacent to the Stade Maurice David, home fans were left almost in disbelief at how their imploding and depleted side somehow still conjured a win.

The French were at one point in the first half down to 11 players after three yellow cards, including one upgraded to a 20-minute red, and a straight red.

A bus fire near the ground delayed the start of the second half. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

It enabled the Wallaroos to power into a 19-0 lead, but that was not enough to stop France fighting back with three second-half tries, even while suffering a sixth card after the break.

Australia, who also had Michaela Leonard sent to the bin in the second half to complete the card chaos, did not help itself as the French reeled off 17 unanswered points in the final 25 minutes to turn a 26-12 deficit into the most unlikely win.

Ultimately, the four Australian tries from Britanny Merlo, Tania Naden, Caitlyn Halse and Piper Duck were not enough for them to follow up last week's comprehensive defeat by England with a morale-boosting win.

The craziness began early, with the French being hit with four cards in 20 minutes, with Ambre Mwayembe, Lea Champon and Lea Murie all binned for high tackles — Mwayembe's being upgraded to a 20-minute red — before Chloe Correa got a straight red for eye-gouging in the maul.

Australia cashed in, with Merlo rolling over from the maul for her second international try after 17 minutes, Naden peeling off to score against a side left helpless when down to 11 and Halse then scoring the Wallaroos' slickest effort after a fine team move.

But when France started getting its numbers back, it became a very different game, as it reduced the deficit to 19-12 by half-time.

After Duck's early score five minutes into the delayed second half, Pauline Bourdon went over to narrow the gap.

When Leonard was binned for a high tackle, the hosts became increasingly encouraged, only to be checked again as Charlotte Escudero got penalised for 10 minutes for her own high challenge.

France then used its maul power to go over for a 68th-minute try through hooker Elisa Riffonneau before Teani Feleu crashed over in the corner for the clincher.

The Wallaroos play in Edinburgh next week against a Scotland side that lost 66-14 to 10-try New Zealand.

title: Photographers' vision for struggling town creates portrait of success
text:
Tell us about your experience.

When a growing number of stores were left empty in the town of Blackall, in western Queensland, graziers Sarah Pearson and Lisa Alexander put their heads together.

It was 2016 and years of drought had taken a financial and emotional toll on the community.

Lisa Alexander and Sarah Pearson's social media campaign became a movement for Blackall. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"[We] decided we need to showcase something big, showcase our area, our community, and we thought if we had community backing, it'd get momentum," Ms Pearson said.

The pair turned to their shared passion of photography, with their #BetterInBlackall social media campaign inspiring the community to take snapshots of the region that were then used to cover empty shop windows.

The Better in Blackall project added eye-catching signs to the town featuring the community's photos. (Supplied: Sarah Pearson)

Ms Pearson said the "flow-on effect" from that one idea over the last 10 years had been incredible, with the campaign triggering a revamp of the town's annual festival and becoming the basis of Blackall's welcome signs.

Quirkiness a valuable commodity for towns

First impressions were of great importance for towns, community consultant Peter Kenyon said.

Peter Kenyon (left) took the Small Town Reinvention Conference on the road in western Queensland. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"Things that we do with our town entrance statements, the state of our main street, what shops do with their window displays, all of those things matter," he said.

"We've got to constantly be looking at our communities with fresh eyes and asking, 'What can we do?'"

For the third National Small Town Reinvention Conference, Mr Kenyon took 80 delegates from around the country on a tour through outback Queensland, visiting eight towns in the central west.

He estimated 70 per cent of small towns were dying but Queensland's outback had bucked the trend.

"If I had to list, for example, the 20 best tourist attractions or events or activities that go on in small towns, at least a dozen of them would be out here in western Queensland."

Attracting people to visit and live in a town is a key issue for many communities. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Mr Kenyon said humour and quirkiness could have a real impact for towns that wanted to reinvent themselves.

"How do we make our community a place where we all want to keep raising our family, where our young people will go off, maybe to uni or travel the world, but want to one day come back and contribute?" he asked.

Councils strengthen local relationships

After moving from the city, Ben Forbes is passionate about strengthening his remote WA community. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Ben Forbes, CEO of Yilgarn Shire Council located between Kalgoorlie and Perth, said he attended in the hope of learning how his community could turn its trajectory around.

"You can talk to anybody that's been there forever and they can remember back in the heyday," he said.

"The wheat belt's in a bit of a slump at the moment."

Mr Forbes used to work in accounting in Perth, but found he was more inspired to use his skills to help a small community.

"I think people are just very genuine out in the country. There's no facade," he said.

"They care about their community."

The Big Yellowbelly project in Isisford was sculpted using local scrap materials. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Isisford's Big Yellowbelly sculpture stood out to him as an example of how a town could unite to tell its story.

"I think more than anything, it's building that shared identity," Mr Forbes said.

"Yilgarn has a lot of really good community members, a lot of little groups, because we're quite geographically spread out.

"So for me, primarily, it's about how can we bring that together into one sort of unified thing."

Community builds on heritage

The Blackall Masonic Lodge wound down in 2016 before its conversion into a cafe. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Blackall-Tambo Regional Council has continued its focus on improving the town's presentation with its Shopfront Renewal Program, which stimulated $315,000 of co-funded investment into landscaping, signage and painting.

Blackall-Tambo Councillor Boyd Johnstone said reinventing a town took the backing of locals.

"You need to have a grassroots push for such projects to be successful."

Boyd Johnstone says grassroots movements can help towns progress. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Cr Johnstone has experience in running with an idea to inject a spark into his community.

When Blackall Masonic Lodge disbanded in 2016, he preserved and restored the heritage-listed building into a cafe, gallery and antique store with his partner Chris Kadel.

"We love our community and sort of just gut instinct knew we would be supported and it was what the community needed," he said.

The former Blackall Masonic Lodge is now a cafe, gallery and antique store. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

He recalled it was over a coffee in the refurbished building with philanthropist Owen Stockwell and Louise Campbell from not-for-profit Red Ridge Interior that an idea was born to preserve the region's cultural items.

The idea has become the ongoing $21 million Blackall Cultural Precinct project funded by the federal government, Blackall-Tambo Council and Red Ridge Interior.

The $21 million Blackall Cultural Precinct is an ongoing project. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

"We now have two giant storage facilities, which have climate-controlled storage containers, fireproof safes. Yeah, it's pretty incredible," Cr Johnstone said.

The town has also harnessed its heritage with the restoration of the Blackall Historical Woolscour and the launch of the Outback Circus Carnival.

title: Five assaulted, bottles thrown at umpires as ugly scenes erupt at tense prelim final

Football fans who threw cans and bottles at umpires face a five-year AFL ban after ugly behaviour boiled over at a tense preliminary final on Saturday night. Loading Dozens of fans flung bottles and cans at the umpires as they walked off the ground after the match. Hawks fans also booed the umpires and vented their frustration over a series of high-stakes decisions in the match’s dying minutes that went the Lions’ way. Two fans were removed for “behaviour incidents” and one for entering without a ticket. “Two men were assaulted as they made their way to leave the venue. The victims were allegedly punched after remonstrating with another spectator,” police said. Another two people told police they were also punched as they were leaving, and a fifth man struck his head on a wall after an alleged push. He was not seriously injured.

In yet another incident, a mother claimed a man threw nachos at her and her son. “It’s absolutely disgusting, and I’m just sick of going out in Melbourne and being worried for my safety,” she told 3AW. If identified, they will be banned from games and the stadium for a minimum of five years.” Cans litter the ground after Hawthorn’s loss to Brisbane. Getty Images Premier Ben Carroll joined the AFL Umpires Association, the Hawks and Jeff Kennett in condemning the ugly scenes that threatened to overshadow perhaps one of the greatest football games this century. Carroll said the throwing of bottles was “not the Victorian way”.

“I think these people should be made an example of. This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head,” Carroll said. “You’ve always got to respect the umpire’s decision.” Former grand final umpire Ray Chamberlain said fans who threw projectiles onto the field should not come back to the football. Umpires dodge projectiles as they exit the ground. AFL Photos via Getty Images The Lions clawed back the lead moments before the final siren when Hawks defender Jarman Impey was pinged for holding the ball and Lion Hugh McCluggage coolly slotted a goal from the resultant free kick. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said he understood the fans’ emotions, but added that “we shouldn’t be throwing things on the field”.

“The emotion of sport, it’s why we love it so much,” he said in his post-match press conference. “All sports, but ours in particular – the beauty is the emotion it makes you feel. At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears. Part of me wanted to scream with rage. It is the best game in the world with 100,000 at the MCG doing its thing, but if you are going to throw stuff, don’t come back,” Chamberlain said. “Have your feelings, have an opinion, be passionate, it is what makes it great. The fans are the single most important ingredient in the whole thing. But if you are going to throw projectiles, don’t come.”

Mitchell was also gently critical of the umpires, saying the Impey decision was not the main one that concerned him. “[There were] a couple leading up to it and other key moments in the game. I’m sure the umpires will assess how they performed in the game in key moments.” Loading Carroll would not be drawn when asked if these comments were appropriate so soon after the ugly crowd reaction. “I thought the umpires did an excellent job, but I don’t think at any level of any sport, umpires can be having projectiles thrown at them because it is just so dangerous.”

Ex-premier and Hawks president Jeff Kennett was at the game, but said he didn’t notice any bottles being thrown as he left on the final siren. He said he saw nothing wrong with Mitchell’s comments. “I didn’t feel it was anything else but measured. You could feel the pain in it: often people give their best speeches when they lose,” he said. “Any throwing of projectiles, whatever they are, in whatever setting, is simply unacceptable.” Cans and bottles on the ground at the MCG. Getty Images AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said on Sunday that he was stunned by the spectacle. “I’ve never seen a collective doing what they did like that,” he told this masthead.

I couldn’t believe what I was seeing.” In a statement, AFL Umpires Association boss Rob Kerr said the actions of sections of the crowd after the siren were completely unacceptable, and welcomed the swift condemnation. “The AFLUA condemns, in the strongest terms, the actions of those supporters who threw bottles and other objects at the umpires as they left the MCG following last night’s preliminary final,” Kerr said. “Umpiring finals football is an enormous responsibility, and the umpires met that challenge with skill and composure throughout an intensely contested match. With a step back against the grain, a shimmy and then a pivot around yet another hapless opponent, Daly Cherry-Evans did what he does best. He finished with a grin, and a giggle, too. Against the Redcliffe-based Dolphins no less, where he took those first furtive steps in rugby league as a six-year-old for Redcliffe more than 30 years ago, where his dad and uncle both played as well? “I completely understand the sentiment, but they are just storylines,” Cherry-Evans said with a smile when his links to the Dolphins were raised. “At the end of the day, we’re playing a prelim … At no stage have we made it about me or anyone who is leaving the club. Because while those things create great headlines, they distract us from what we need to do here, which is play footy.” Loading Cherry-Evans, throughout an enthralling 16-year, 377-game career (which pushes well past 400 appearances when 21 Tests and 26 Origins are included), often inadvertently, so often has. Few have provided such regular, meaty copy.

And as for the Redcliffe connections, the 30-year-old archived photos do more justice than words ever could. In more recent times, the Dolphins have eyed off that cherub-cheeked kid more than once as a potential star signing. In 2021, when he still could, Manly owner Scott Penn issued a “hands off” edict as Redcliffe hunted culture-setting marquee signings while establishing their first NRL roster. When things fell apart between the Sea Eagles and Cherry-Evans, the Dolphins were one of the few clubs the veteran No.7 actually met with and weighed up as an option, though the Roosters were always early clubhouse leaders for his signature. A young Daly Cherry-Evans (fourth from right) with his father, Troy (red jacket, back row) in 1996. Now, after more than 33,000 minutes of top-level rugby league (80 x 424 games, you can work out all the extra time), Cherry-Evans now has just either 80 or 160 minutes left in the NRL.

By his own admission, he was sub-par against Penrith in the Roosters’ 19-12 week one finals loss. No one has slotted more field goals than Cherry-Evans’ 31 in the NRL era. But the late attempt he shanked – by his lofty standards, oh so badly – was, according to Fox Sports stats, the 50th missed one-pointer of his career, too. It doesn’t matter in the wash of a truly glittering career. Except for the explanation Cherry-Evans offers after getting back to his best against Cronulla, with that crucial 27th minute solo try and three try assists as well. “You won’t find anyone harder on my own game than myself. It’s as simple as that,” he said after being the last Rooster to emerge from Allianz Stadium. “But what happens next is if I carry my divots, I’m then not only putting myself out, but my team out [too]. From the words of the great Ted Lasso, memory of a goldfish.”

That selective memory – “sporting amnesia” as Trent Robinson dubbed it on Saturday night – was perfect for jettisoning the attacking missteps against Penrith. Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Confident’: Walker eyes remarkable return as DCE sets up storybook Dolphins clash Less so, the way the Dolphins pulled his right-side defensive combination with Rob Toia apart in their last clash. In a 26-12 victory for the Queenslanders, one that announced their arrival as proper premiership contenders, they went after Cherry-Evans and no doubt plan to do so again on Friday night. The Roosters’ right edge has been a work in progress all season. Halves are naturally targeted; Cherry-Evans as much as any. Yet, while the Roosters scored eight tries to Cronulla’s two at Allianz Stadium, the Sharks weren’t able to exploit the veteran No.7, despite having more tackles (38-27) inside the opposition 20-metre zone. “Defence wins you competitions there’s no doubt about it,” Cherry-Evans said.

title: Activist group using AI to flood ABC with thousands of bias complaints
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive BusinessCompaniesMiddle East tensions Activist group using AI to flood ABC with thousands of bias complaints Calum Jaspan September 20, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Activist groups are using artificial intelligence to target the ABC’s coverage of the Middle East with accusations of bias, contributing to a sharp rise in the number of coordinated complaints detected by the public broadcaster’s independent ombudsman. One of those groups is Pen Power Australia, which has been using AI technology to coordinate complaints to the ABC’s board and management to attempt to correct what it sees as bias and make coverage more favourable to Israel. Institutions such as the ABC are grappling with large numbers of complaints that activist groups are coordinating through tech platforms. Sam Mooy A new report released by the ABC’s Ombudsman on Thursday found that organised complaint campaigns rose sharply over the past year, in part due to the assistance of artificial intelligence. The report did not name Pen Power, but ABC ombudsman Fiona Cameron identified 48 “campaigns” during the year ending June 30 which accounted for 5259 total complaints, or 61 per cent of all content complaints received.

Advertisement

“Complaints were categorised as campaigns where a concentration of complaints raised similar concerns about the same content within a specific period. They may be substantively similar or identically worded or appear coordinated,” the ombudsman’s report notes. The report underscores how coordinated campaigns are making it more difficult for organisations like the ABC to gauge the level of community anger over hot-button issues such as the Middle East as they seek to balance genuine engagement with resisting pressure campaigns. Pen Power’s coordinator John Grimwade said the campaigns he had organised could have anything from 100 people to a few thousand sending complaint letters if he could enlist support from overseas groups. The group runs campaigns about Gaza, Israel and anything connected to these issues, he said. Last month, Grimwade told the group its members had sent more than 40,000 letters by email to date, according to internal WhatsApp messages seen by this masthead. “Our campaigns go out as required,” Grimwade said. “We try to keep up with the ABC in particular but so many of their reports are biased or statements made that lack proper context.”

Advertisement

Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu’s rivals call him ‘unfit’ for office after report he was warned of October 7 attack In March, ABC chair Kim Williams defended the broadcaster against accusations of bias, saying it stood by its coverage of the conflict in the Middle East. Grimwade, an Adelaide retiree, confirmed the group has used a platform called Activist Mailer, which boasts online of letting users coordinate campaigns with artificial intelligence. The platform’s website claims that its platform makes what would otherwise appear as a barrage of emails appear “unique” by using different words, tone, formating and length to deliver the same coordinated message, “each sent directly from supporters’ own inboxes”. “The result? Messages that get read, voices that get heard, and movements that drive real change.”

Advertisement

But Grimwade is planning on changing to a new AI platform. “I am currently using the Activist Mailer but will be changing most of our campaigns over to the new AI,” Grimwade said. Letter-writing campaigns have worked in the past. In late 2023, the ABC sacked casual radio host Antoinette Lattouf after a coordinated letter-writing campaign targeted members of the broadcaster’s board and management team, including then-chair Ita Buttrose. That campaign was driven by a separate pro-Israel group and did not include Pen Power Australia. A Federal Court judge last year found the ABC had sacked Lattouf unlawfully and she was awarded $150,000 in damages. The case cost the ABC more than $2 million. Grimwade said his campaigns had had little success so far beyond yielding a response from ABC head of editorial standards Gavin Fang or the ombudsman. “In simple terms, they think they are right,” he said. But he said Pen Power had succeeded in getting an Instagram video removed in recent days featuring Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran covering the Iran war.

Advertisement

“We have had a video on Instagram taken down, which we are claiming as a win,” Grimwade said. “It was removed shortly after our letters were starting to be sent.” Related Article Media & marketing ABC slams watchdog finding that Four Corners program failed impartiality test In a statement, an ABC spokesperson said the video had already been taken down before the first campaign email came in because the reporter misread the script, resulting in an error. “In any event, the campaign would have been immaterial because when we identify errors, we always take action,” the spokesperson said. In a podcast interview with the conservative Australian Jewish Association, Grimwade claimed his campaigns had more success outside the ABC. Pen Power last week organised a campaign of emails to the ABC managing director Hugh Marks, chair Kim Williams and Fang, claiming the ABC’s reporting on Israel-Palestine was inaccurate and not impartial.

Advertisement

“As long as it’s antisemitic, we’ll have a go,” Grimwade told AJA chief executive Robert Gregory. Gregory praised Grimwade and thanked him “for the work you’re doing”. The two organisations have a “limited” partnership, Grimwade confirmed. In another call-out this week, Pen Power produced a letter asking members to target the ABC over its Middle Eastern guidance document. “Please join with us and send the letter exposing it for what it really is. Another ABC document that is bias [sic] and factually incorrect,” the message said. It isn’t just Australian groups pushing these coordinated campaigns, Grimwade said. “I am aware of overseas groups doing the same as us and we sometimes use each other’s letters where it’s applicable to do so,” he said, without naming his international allies. “The only other Australian group is a WhatsApp chat group that was formed specifically to tackle the ABC problem.” The ombudsman said 1148 (13 per cent of all content complaints) related to the Israel-Palestine conflict. The volume of allegations of both pro-Israel or pro-Palestine coverage were about equal, the report said.

Advertisement

But allegations of pro-Iranian coverage topped both allegations of pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian coverage. The US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. The ABC received 2746 complaints from across the globe about an Instagram reel published in May, focusing on its reporting from inside Iran. Most complaints were made by “Iranian Australians” or “Iranians in the diaspora community” the ombudsman said, and alleged the post lacked impartiality. The ombudsman also noted “68 identical complaints by email to the ABC board and other recipients (rather than the ABC complaints form)” regarding an April episode of Radio National program If You’re Listening about the war in Iran. The identical complaints said the episode presented Iran as a “reasonable diplomatic partner” and Israel as an “antagonist” and “disruptor of diplomacy”, suggesting a lack of impartiality, the ombudsman’s report, which cleared the piece of content of any breaches, said. The ombudsman has since changed its classification of complaints it identifies as identical or coordinated, counting them as one complaint. There was something almost The Truman Show about Anthony Albanese’s Californian morning at Apple Park. The prime minister had travelled to the heart of Silicon Valley to meet Tim Cook – or, as Donald Trump once called him, “Tim Apple” – and spruik Australia’s world-leading crackdown on social media for under-16s. The prime minister gets a demonstration of Apple’s new child safety features at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer If only Ed Harris had wandered into shot to tell him the whole thing was a set. Instead, there was the enormous circular Apple “Spaceship” headquarters with its carbon-sink oak forest across 70 hectares, with olive groves, roaming coyotes, gleaming glass and enough security to ensure the travelling journalists saw only the parts of the $5 billon compound that Apple wanted them to see.

The media pack was briefly allowed inside the foyer for a child-friendly product demonstration of Apple’s latest products, including the new foldable Duo phone. It’s just $3499. But the meeting was off limits. No cameras nor photographs, not even pictures of the buildings or Apple employees. The journalists could look, but they could not record. Not even a sighting of the cult leader. Welcome to the world of “Tim Apple”, complete with the Steve Jobs Memorial Theatre. Albanese spent an hour behind closed doors with Cook and the Apple executive team, continuing a relationship that began when the Apple boss called him in June to discuss the company’s new child-safety controls. Cook had told Albanese the changes were partly inspired by Australia’s world-leading social media age ban, as well as Apple’s own research into the effects of social media on children.
