Now the bromance was rekindled at Apple Park. Tech brothers from another mother. Apple executive chairman Tim Cook with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese on x.com Cook later posted that he was grateful to welcome @AlboMP to Apple Park to discuss the company’s “longstanding commitment to Australia” and its latest innovations to help keep children safe online. Albanese, who rarely meets a celebrity without an obligatory for a selfie, was even more effusive. He said it was a “proud moment” to have the head of a company that had “changed the world” recognise Australia’s leadership in protecting children from the negative consequences of technology.

Related Article Updated

AI Albanese urges US, China to strike AI deal akin to nuclear non-proliferation treaty Apple’s new controls allow parents to limit the time children spend on particular apps and devices, restrict who can message them and introduce other safeguards. There was, however, a rather obvious irony hanging over the morning. As one wag in the journalist pack observed that the scene was a bit like McDonald’s selling shots of Ozempic as part of a meal deal. Apple is, after all, one of the companies most responsible for putting a powerful computer in the pockets of just about every adult – and an increasingly large number of children. Albanese was at pains to say this was not a war on technology.

Advertisement

The iPhone and Apple’s products had delivered “enormous benefits”, he said, while artificial intelligence could improve healthcare, including cancer detection and diagnosis. The task, in the prime minister’s telling, was to make sure people remained in control. View post on X That argument will be central to Albanese’s international push on artificial intelligence as he prepares for talks at the United Nations. He also discussed the government’s proposed “My Feed, My Way” reforms, which would give users greater control over the algorithms to determine what appears in their social media feeds.

So there was Albanese, inside Apple’s perfectly manicured technological utopia, making the case for putting some boundaries around the machines. All while thanking them for all that they do. Then, naturally, it was time to leave via the merchandise store. Mugs, pens, notebooks and water bottles with an Apple logo. Onesies for your loved ones, and 16 T-shirts to choose from. In the movie, Truman escapes the simulation. In Cupertino, the tech giant selling the digital poison is now selling the antidote, too. title: Three contentious free kicks, one crazy minute: The detailed verdict on preliminary final umpiring calls
text:
Advertisement

Loading

The skills of the players in this intense, classic preliminary final between Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions were the real highlight but when three free kicks are paid in the final 61 seconds and the lead changes those umpiring decisions will be examined and reviewed in fine detail. Football writers Peter Ryan, Marc McGowan and former AFL grand final umpire “Razor” Ray Chamberlain took a close look at the final three free kicks to the Brisbane Lions and whether they were justified. 1. Lewis shows insufficient intent (62 seconds remaining) Peter Ryan says: The only query is whether a free kick would be paid in the first minute of a game, but beyond that, there is no doubt it was a free kick. The AFL clarified the rule after round two this season in a memo to clubs, which basically said a token effort to touch the ball before it went out of bounds would be insufficient intent. Mitch Lewis would have got away with it if he’d either grabbed the ball and momentum took him out or made a genuine attempt to keep the ball in play (which is difficult as he would have risked missing the ball). It’s a fair call. And remember Lewis hardly fumbled all match. His response to the decision was very professional.

Advertisement

Marc McGowan says: Lewis wasn’t trying to keep the ball in play. AFL headquarters made it clear early in the season that simply attempting to touch the ball to avoid a “lasso” free kick would no longer suffice, so as harsh as this seems, the umpire made the correct call. Ray Chamberlain says: The action of Lewis is all that matters when it comes to insufficient intent, but for context, Jack Ginnivan kicks an end-over-end grubber along the boundary line. If it goes out of bounds without being touched it is a last-disposal free kick. Lewis has to show sufficient intent to keep the ball in play. Has the Lewis’ action demonstrated sufficient intent to keep the ball in play? No. The umpire made the correct call. 2. Zorko cops high contact (53 seconds remaining)

Advertisement

Peter Ryan says: Tiggy touch wood, but high contact was made and many of those are paid or not paid during a season depending on what the umpire sees. Josh Weddle’s arms made contact with Dayne Zorko above the shoulder, so it is a free kick. Marc McGowan says: Glancing blow or not, it is crystal clear that Josh Weddle made high contact to Dayne Zorko while coming from the opposite direction as the veteran Lion spun around. Would there be any controversy if Zorko had done this to Weddle? Ray Chamberlain says: There is certainly high contact. He is not decapitated by any stretch, but you can’t make high contact. He has flicked him across the face. It is going to get paid. Impey caught holding the ball

Advertisement

Peter Ryan says: Great decision by the umpire. When Jarman Impey takes possession of the ball, he has both arms free momentarily. It gives him a second where he could have handballed or kicked the ball, but he decided to do neither. Hugh McCluggage’s tackle was outstanding for the situation. After holding Impey for about a second around the waist, he then latched on to his hand, so the Hawks’ defender couldn’t handball either, making kicking Impey’s only option. The Hawk just froze and hoped the umpire would not be brave enough to pay holding the ball. Four seconds lapsed between taking possession and the decision being made. Marc McGowan says: Hugh McCluggage was brilliant, and Jarman Impey was not. The umpire was equally good. You can also effectively forget whether Impey had an initial opportunity with both arms available. McCluggage executed a tackle as players are taught – pin one arm, and remove half the options. In this scenario, Impey needed to be saved by a third party instantly coming in, or he had to attempt to get a kick away far earlier than he did. The risk was he would drop the ball and not get a foot to it, but Impey’s feigned efforts to dispose the ball were never going to be enough. Brave call, and right call. Ray Chamberlain says: The law has to line up before any decision is made with the umpire correctly assessing there was no prior opportunity, a legal tackle had been laid and the ball had not been pinned. But then there is what I call “a cadence piece” which is a question of how long do you give the player [to dispose of the ball]. If it is pinned and he can’t dispose of the ball or he is unable to make a genuine attempt, then you can call for a ball up, but if not, as is the case here, then it is free kick against Impey for holding the ball. Bravo to the umpire.

Advertisement

And for the record ... Not only were all three free kicks above the correct decisions, but Hawthorn were fortunate with non-calls on the Jacks, Ginnivan and Gunston, in the dying minutes. Mitch Lewis’ forward-50 hanger with three-and-a-half minutes to go, which would have gone down in club folklore if they won, followed Gunston shoving Harris Andrews in the back, forcefully enough that he could not contest the ball.

Advertisement

The other damning factor? Gunston’s arms were extended as he did it, so he was lucky not to cost Lewis his brilliant mark. There was another with about two-and-a-half minutes left. After Harry Morrison’s shocking turnover to Zac Bailey, which was a clear mark, Ginnivan wrenched the ball off Bailey then handballed over his head.

As Hawthorn snatched the lead in a pulsating final three minutes of a preliminary final for the ages, Oscar Allen accepted his brave move across the country 12 months earlier had fallen a week short of his dream. Nor did he feel a sense of vindication for handing in the Eagles captaincy last year, amid ongoing media speculation, and departing his native Western Australia for Brisbane. Loading “Even without the on-field team success, like the way they made me feel welcome in this group – not only me, but my wife and my family – you can see why they’ve been so successful,” Allen said. “It’s such a great culture and great people. Jacques Heim is a charismatic talker who uses your name for emphasis and delights in outrageous comments. He’s a natural showman, boyish for his 62 years, with the self-possession of a practised rule breaker. “Nick, I have to tell you, I was never a dancer, I was never a gymnast. I was never an acrobat,” he says in French-accented English. Escape is a spectacular production from Los Angeles playing Brisbane Festival. George Simian “I was a rebel, I was a punk, I got kicked out of six different schools in Paris. I was a little wild and so they had to put me in jail for a while, and then they let me go.

Advertisement

“So my family told me: ‘Jacques, you need to leave, you need to go to the land of opportunity, America.’ So I said ‘great’.” Heim is the founder and creative director of Diavolo: Architecture in Motion, a Los Angeles-based company bringing its daredevil style of performance to Australia for the Brisbane Festival. The company’s spectacular dance pieces involve huge geometric props that roll, pivot and swing while the performers climb, balance, hang, fall and jump. “This is something I will remember, it was incredible, congratulations,” Simon Cowell told the company after its debut on America’s Got Talent in 2017. (Diavolo would go on to be finalists.)

Advertisement

Surprise and delight are arguably in Heim’s blood: his grandfather and namesake was an influential couturier who shocked the postwar fashion world with his two-piece swimsuit the Atome – the forerunner of the bikini – and pioneered prêt-a-porter (ready to wear) clothing. “I guess some of my artistic juice came from him,” Heim says. “I’m really interested about what is innovation, how do you know if an idea is a good idea, how does it affect people?” Heim’s company performed in a routine with Dua Lipa at the 2024 Grammys. George Simian As the headline act for Brisbane Festival the company is presenting Escape, a show with 22 performers that “follows a group of humans as they … escape from their ordinary lives into a surreal landscape of infinite possibilities”. “The seed of the show started as revolting against the state of the world that we live in,” Heim says.

Advertisement

“You know what’s going on in the States. It’s a little crazy, especially with the government, who completely cancel every aspect of the arts.” (The Trump administration cut funding to the National Endowment for the Arts in 2025.) Related Article ★★★★

Entertainment Cirque in a grass skirt: Fijian Flying Circus gives aerial acrobatics a Pacific island twist “The reason it’s called Escape is very simply because we wanted to escape this crazy world that we live in, in the United States.” Heim does not need much encouragement to say what life is like in the country that has been his home for more than three decades. “When we were creating and rehearsing Escape, we had the ICE agents actually moving around our studio...

Advertisement

“I love America. I don’t want to be a hypocrite because it has given me so much opportunity, but I do have to say in a very genuine way: it’s not the same country.” Back in his punk days, in 1983, Heim attended liberal arts college Middlebury in Vermont, and started getting interested in acting. But his garbled English was holding him back, so when friends suggested he try dance instead something clicked. Performances skirt danger and are timed down to the millisecond. George Simian Architecture was another love, and he began to see parallels, formulating a style of prop-based movement that was not quite dance, not quite circus, and not quite acrobatics. Heim created Diavolo on graduating in dance from CalArts, and its first full-length show debuted in 1999.

Advertisement

By 2005, Heim was high profile enough to be invited to direct Cirque du Soleil’s show Kà, which is still running at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. “That was my PhD, because I learned a lot. I nearly got fired at least 34 times,” he quips. He is adamant that Diavolo is “not a circus company”. The distinction is a philosophical one: circus acts can involve danger, whereas danger, for Diavolo, is a “theme”. “I need to put my performers in a danger zone on purpose. Because when you put a group of people into a state of survival, they come closer together and help one another, they don’t think about themselves, but they think about others and how to create safety around each other. “So we have major safety protocols, and we have many steps that we implement.”

Advertisement

Pushing performers beyond their physical and emotional limits has been a feature of Heim’s performance workshops with military veterans, a program Diavolo launched in 2016 as a way of treating PTSD. Related Article Film & TV production Only heartstrings attached: Jim Henson and the evolving magic of puppetry “I operate as a drill sergeant. Even if some of the veterans are in a wheelchair, I ask them, can you get out of your wheelchair? Can you crawl? I make them crawl and move with all the dancers that elevate them.” Veterans have reported that taking part helped them avert self-harm. Heim received a Meritorious Civilian Service Medal for the program. He says his company is looking forward to performing in Brisbane for the first time, having previously appeared at the Arts Centre Melbourne in 2014.

“I hope my dancers will not defect and stay, because I have to tell you, Australia is a great country, has a lot of great arts. I won’t be surprised if some of my dancers decide to defect. “Who knows, Nick, maybe I will move the company to Australia, and I will never leave Brisbane?” I mention that the far right is on the rise in Australia too, and may have something to say about that. “Is it? It’s weird, because it’s happening in one country after the other ... No one is really safe today in 2026. “So how do we find equilibrium? How do we find a sense of hope? It’s about being together, it’s about creating a community. That was the core of Escape that we created among our 22 performers: a sense of community.

Advertisement

“At the end of the day, Nick, we’re from the same family called humans, and how can we support and help one another?” Escape runs at the Playhouse, QPAC, September 23-27.

title: Australia wants a seat at the UN's most powerful table. What power would it yield?
text:
IN BRIEF Australia is campaigning for a seat on the UN body responsible for international peace and security.

A seat would give Australia a vote and role in key negotiations, but not the veto held by five permanent members.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is heading to New York with a diplomatic pitch that has been more than a decade in the making: Putting Australia back on the United Nations Security Council.

Australia is campaigning for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2029-30, which would mark its first stint on the powerful UN body since 2014.

The government says a seat would give Australia a stronger voice on decisions affecting the country and the region.

Australia's campaign is expected to focus on issues including artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety, as well as climate action, international law and support for Pacific nations.

But what exactly does the UN Security Council do, and what would Australia gain by being on it?

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is the UN Security Council?

The Security Council is one of the six main bodies of the United Nations and has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.

It is made up of 15 countries, each with one vote.

Five of them — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — are permanent members, while another 10 countries are elected by the UN General Assembly to serve two-year terms.

Unlike most other UN bodies, the Security Council can make decisions that member states are obligated to implement.

READ MORE We came to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos

It can impose sanctions, establish peacekeeping operations and, in some circumstances, authorise the use of force. It can also investigate disputes, call for peaceful settlements and make recommendations aimed at maintaining or restoring international peace and security.

For a substantive resolution to pass, it needs at least nine votes.

And there is an important catch — each of the five permanent members has veto power, meaning a negative vote from any one of them can block a substantive resolution even if it otherwise has enough support.

Australia would not gain that veto power if elected, as it belongs exclusively to the five permanent members of the Security Council.

Non-permanent members such as Australia have the same single vote on council decisions, but cannot unilaterally block a substantive resolution.

So what would Australia actually gain?

While a non-permanent seat does not come with a veto, it gives countries a direct role in decisions they would otherwise largely have to influence from outside the council.

Australia would have a vote on Security Council decisions and be involved in negotiating resolutions and other outcomes on conflicts and security crises around the world.

It would also take part in closed meetings and consultations between council members and could chair subsidiary bodies, including sanctions committees.

Every member also takes a turn holding the presidency of the Security Council for one calendar month, allowing them to preside over meetings and help shape the council's program of work.

Australia's previous term shows the practical difference membership can make.

During 2013-14, Australia participated in hundreds of council meetings, including closed meetings available only to members, and was closely involved in negotiating dozens of resolutions and presidential statements.

Its seat became particularly significant following the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, which killed 298 people, including 38 Australian citizens and residents.

Australia authored and led negotiations on Security Council Resolution 2166, which was unanimously adopted four days after the crash.

The resolution condemned the downing of the plane, called for a full and independent investigation and demanded access to the crash site.

Australia also used its term to work on humanitarian access in Syria, counter-terrorism, small arms and the protection of civilians.

Why does Australia want a seat again?

The government argues that Australia's security and prosperity depend on an international system in which countries follow agreed rules and work collectively on global problems.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said a seat would give Australia "a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region", describing the country as an active middle power with a role to play in international peace and security.

The bid is also increasingly focused on what Australia argues will be emerging security challenges by the time it takes up the seat.

Technology is expected to be central to the campaign, with the government arguing that artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security.

Speaking at a Security Council debate last year, Wong said AI had the potential to transform conflict and diplomacy and argued the council should play a role in developing international rules and norms around its use.

She said Australia's experience in digital infrastructure and technology partnerships would form part of what it could bring to the council.

Australia's broader foreign policy priorities, including the Pacific, climate change, protecting civilians and supporting international law, are also expected to feature in the campaign.

How does Australia get elected?

Australia cannot simply nominate itself and take a seat.

The 10 non-permanent positions are distributed between regional groupings, with five seats coming up for election each year.

Australia belongs to the Western European and Others Group, or WEOG, and is seeking one of the group's two seats available for the 2029-30 term.

So far, Australia and Finland are the only candidates for those two positions, meaning the positions are currently uncontested.

But Australia must still win the support of two-thirds of UN General Assembly members present and voting when the election is held in June 2028.

If all 193 UN member states were present and voted, that would mean securing around 129 votes.

It helps explain why the government is campaigning years before Australia would actually take its seat.

The bid itself is not new. It was first announced in 2015 under the former Coalition government, following Australia's previous stint on the council.

Australia has served five terms on the Security Council since the UN was established, most recently in 2013-14.

A sixth term would not give Australia the power enjoyed by the council's five permanent members.

But for two years, it would give Australia something it otherwise does not have: a seat, a vote and a direct role in negotiations at the UN body responsible for some of the world's most consequential decisions on peace and security.

title: John Farnham to skip tribute concert amid worsening health, family says

In brief Australian and international music stars are due to perform at a John Farnham tribute concert.

Farnham would have loved to attend a tribute concert in his honour, his family says.

John Farnham's tribute concert will go ahead without him as the Australian music legend's family reveals his health has deteriorated.

The music-industry giant will be honoured by local and international performing greats at a blockbuster charity gig at Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena on Sunday, raising funds for the cancer support services that helped him through his own battle with the disease.

The 77-year-old, who has undergone several surgeries for oral cancer, now requires continuous oxygen support and 24-hour care.

A day before the sold-out event, Farnham's wife Jill and the couple's sons Robert and James, said they were "deeply moved by everything happening" at Rod Laver Arena.

title: We came to the Apple mothership to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos and a silent movie

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spent an hour on Sunday (AEST) with former Apple chief Tim Cook at the company's mothership, doing a walk and talk through the famed infinite circle gardens in the heart of Silicon Valley and getting a demonstration of the tech juggernaut’s new parental controls.

Apple’s strict management of media access meant there was no invitation for Australian press cameras to capture the moment Albanese says he was lauded by the director of Apple’s board and credited with driving international efforts to keep kids off social media.

Just a handful of still photographs and a 27-second compilation of silent video were cleared and circulated by the Prime Minister’s Office, showing his interactions with the cult figure, who has a devoted following in the tech world.

Even during a demonstration of the products and controls for Aussie journalists, the company’s media minders asked us not to show the faces of Apple employees, record audio, or publish any further pictures of the inside of the building.

The whole experience aligned with Apple’s famously protective approach to independent media roaming its facilities and its wish to impose privacy measures on its internal workings, from the architecture to the acoustics.

title: The future of this Australian island is in danger. How its residents are fighting back
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Yessie Mosby paces down the beach near his home on Masig, a teardrop-shaped island in the Torres Strait.

As he walks, he points to the crimson fruit of a wongai tree, a marooned yellow rowboat and a tree trunk full of hiding holes — hallmarks of his generations-long connection to this spot.

But not all Mosby's memories are fond.

The Kulkalgal man recalls a day in 2017, when his son recovered the washed-up remains of his great-great-grandmother while playing in the sand.

"They were picking up her bones like shells off the beach. My son grabbed her skull and placed her in a bucket," he says.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Less than three metres above sea level, Masig's sandy shores are slowly being eaten away by rising tides. Areas once safely inland, such as burial sites, playgrounds, roads and family gardens, are receding before its residents' eyes.

The most dire scientific predictions give the Torres Strait's low-lying islands, including Masig, until 2050 before they become uninhabitable. But Mosby, a climate advocate and chair of the Masigalgal Prescribed Body Corporate (a legal entity that holds and manages native title rights on behalf of Traditional Owners), has taken to measuring the encroaching tides in real time.

"When I was young, the island was here," the 43-year-old says, using the sand as a slate to draw a line.

One of Yessie Mosby's sons scours a beach at Masig, where the remains of his ancestor washed ashore. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

But with the birth of each of his seven children, now aged five to 15 years, that mark has edged further inland.

Finding his ancestor's remains was the final straw.

"That loved one should be resting in peace. She shouldn't be washed out into the sea," he says.

That's when it hit me. I have to try and do something to save this place.

Five years later, in 2022, Mosby was among eight Torres Strait Islanders who won a landmark UN human rights ruling against the Australian government over climate change inaction. The group have been calling for urgent action to protect Masig and its neighbouring islands.

Over the past decade, the federal and Queensland governments have invested millions in the Torres Strait Seawalls Program, installing thousands of sandbags to mitigate coastal erosion. On Masig, they wrap around the island's northwestern side to form a seawall.

But so far, external efforts to hold back the tide have been inadequate.

Masig's shorelines are under threat due to rising levels. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

One way Traditional Owners are seeking to take back control of their future is by establishing a new Indigenous Protected Area (IPA). Unlike other conservation zones, such as national parks or marine reserves, IPAs are voluntarily declared and managed by First Nations Australians.

In 2025, the Masigilgal IPA was created to shelter fragile reef systems, culturally significant species and ancient knowledge from the onslaught of climate change. Officially, it covers the 11 uninhabited coral cays surrounding Masig, but much of the conservation work extends to the island too.

Mosby hopes it will give Masigalgal people, the Traditional Owners of Masig, an advantage in the race to save the island.

"We have the Western knowledge of how climate change works [with] traditional knowledge of how the tide runs, the current flows, what occupies these islands, how the island actually sits," he says.

'It was just bare'

Formerly known as Yorke Island, Masig is a coral cay in the Torres Strait's Central Islands cluster. It is situated closer to Papua New Guinea than Australia and is home to just under 300 people.

Masig Island sits around 77km from Papua New Guinea's coastline. Source: SBS News

Life on Masig is unhurried. It has one narrow landing strip, one supermarket, one primary school and one cafe — MigiYarn Cafe. It's been operating for nearly a decade and is the go-to watering hole for locals to meet and chat.

It's been operating for nearly a decade, but this year, the cafe has cemented itself as the go-to watering hole for locals to meet and chat. Beyond the sound of its swaying hammocks and whirring coffee machine, the lapping ocean is never far away, and a constant reminder of the risks of running a beachfront business on Masig.

Everyone here has a story about climate change. Kimiko Mosby, the cafe's co-owner, recalls a particularly extreme bout of weather in 2018.

"We had the high tides, we had the winds, and we had rain. It was just bang, bang, bang," she says.

"It took a few metres from us."

Kimiko Mosby was involved in the consultation process to establish Masig's Indigenous Protected Area. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Mosby had just planted some coconut trees in front of the cafe, which were swept away overnight.

"It was just bare."

So when the opportunity arose to help shape the island's IPA, Mosby jumped at it.

"The consultation process nutted out exactly what we wanted, our input, what our aspirations were, how we saw it and how we wanted to manage it," she says.

After eight years of planning, the Masigilgal IPA was dedicated in July 2025 and now covers 245 hectares of land.

"It's funny, because we always knew Masig and the surrounding islands belong to us, but local people now have a hand in managing our places," she says.

READ MORE Denis watched his ancestral lands be ravaged as a kid. It sparked a major change

The IPA is run by a small group of environmental rangers from the Torres Strait Regional Authority (TSRA), a Commonwealth agency. Most of these rangers are Masigalgal, or from neighbouring islands, and have become "a vital part of our community," Mosby says.

Revegetation and 'the tree of life'

Life on Masig has traditionally revolved around its trove of ocean goods — from historic pearling and shell trades to modern crayfish and prawn exports. But one resource offers hope for the future.

Known locally as 'the tree of life', and in Miriam Mir (a traditional language of the eastern Torres Strait) as "urab", coconut palms are ubiquitous on Masig — so much so that glaring yellow signs warn passersby of falling coconuts.

At a revegetation site on the island's northwestern side, palms of all heights shoot toward the sky, their fibrous roots holding loose sand and soil in place and helping to buffer against erosion.

Coconut palms are abundant on Masig and are known by the traditional name 'urub'. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Laura Pearson, a Kulkalayg woman and senior ranger supervisor from nearby Warraber Island, is working at the site and explains how they collect ripe, unhusked coconuts and strategically replant them when sprouts form.

"Urab is a really culturally significant plant for us Torres Strait people that provides shelter, slows down the coastal erosion effects, and provides us with water and cooking resources," she says.

The approach is tailored to the island's climate and customs.

"It's important to read our traditional seasons," Pearson says.

Unlike the Western seasonal calendar, the timing and duration of seasons vary according to Masig's traditional calendar. Masigalgal people recognise four seasons — Kuki, Zei, Woerr and Naigai — and look for signs in the wind, weather and wildlife to tell them when one season is expected to change to another.

For example, the season of Kuki — which runs roughly December to April — can be read through signs such as the build-up of big storm clouds and lightning in the far north-west. It's a season when Weiba (rose-crowned fruit doves) become fat and plentiful because of the abundance of ripe fruit on the island.

Laura Pearson travels from the nearby Warraber island to work on Masig's revegetation site. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

When SBS News visits, it's leading up to the dry season, which typically runs from September to November.

"We call it Naigai season," Pearson says.

"We don't plant in the dry season; we plant leading up to the monsoon season."

Other native plants are propagated at Mother's Well, the island's plant nursery where rows of green saplings line a polytunnel. Some plants are distributed to community gardens, while others are transported to the IPA's uninhabited islands to boost habitat for local wildlife.

The Masigilgal IPA is a resting spot for more than 30 migratory bird species — including the Eastern Curlew, the world's largest migratory shorebird. According to the Australian Conservation Foundation, global populations have declined by around 80 per cent in the last 30 years. In Australia, the species is now listed as critically endangered due to severe habitat destruction.

The IPA's polytunnel is an incubator for young coconut palm seedlings. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Revegetation is a small part of the management puzzle across Masig's uninhabited islands. Rangers must also tackle marine debris, ghost nets (discarded fishing nets), invasive plants and feral species. A day's work might involve dealing with an outbreak of leucaena, a rapidly growing woody weed, or wild pigs that disturb sacred sites, says Pearson.

"Our job is to get in and eradicate it or control it," she says.

"It's never-ending, but it's the best job in the world."

Beyond Masig

Masigilgal is one of five IPAs scattered throughout the more than 274 islands in the Torres Strait. All IPAs are on uninhabited islands covered by Native Title, many of which were historically used for temporary camps and seasonal hunting. As part of the national IPA program, they receive federal government funding to fuel conservation work.

Nationally, more than 95 IPAs span Land and Sea Country from the Tiwi Islands to Tasmania. But Ilana Foster, TSRA's IPA and traditional knowledge specialist, says that navigating a vast body of ocean poses different challenges to mainland Australia.

Sitting where the Coral and Arafura Seas converge, the Strait is the unofficial dugong capital of the world – more than 100,000 of the marine mammals reside in its vast seagrass meadows. It also harbours six of the world's seven turtle species, three of which regularly nest on islands in the region.

However, sea-level rise is beginning to disturb these patterns.

"The high tides are eating away at the sand beaches, so the amount of ground that turtles have to lay in is reduced," Foster says.

Rangers carry out routine marine surveys, checking for changes and deformities in the number of turtle eggs in a nest, called a clutch.

Some IPAs are also facing existential threats, says Vic McGrath, the Torres Strait's first IPA coordinator.

The Masigilgal IPA is one of 95 IPAs across Australia, but it faces unique challenges due to rising seas. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Warul Kawa (or Deliverance Island), an IPA in the far north-western corner of the Torres Strait, is steeped in spiritual significance.

"When you die, all Torres Strait Islanders go there. Your soul heads off to its final place in the west," McGrath explains.

But this sacred island and its IPA are facing a multitude of risks, from shipping lanes and oil spills to the growing threat of illegal fishing.

"Some of those newer IPAs are based on little islands adjacent to shipping channels. I'm concerned about modern impacts", he says.

Amid these dangers, Foster says rangers are documenting vital cultural data.

The reality is that these places are disappearing.

"What else can you do when something is gone but look back on images, recordings, written works," she says.

Since 2009, TSRA's traditional ecological knowledge program has recorded the names of local flora and fauna. Previously, this information had been passed down orally or chronicled in outdated Western anthropological studies, notably from an 1800s historic expedition by AC Haddon.

Now, these community resources developed via the IPA act as a benchmark for monitoring change.

"You can see that the seasons have changed significantly, that they're not happening at the same time," Foster says.

It takes a village

For now, First Nations-led solutions are shouldering a heavy burden.

At Yessie Mosby's camp, rangers have provided makeshift buffers made from densely packed coconut fibres to help fortify the shoreline.

"It's working. I reckon if this wasn't here, this tree would've been washed out," he says.

Sandbags are being used on Masig to prevent further coastal erosion. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

At times, it can feel like paddling upstream.

Mosby points out that Masig has a tiny carbon footprint, and despite their best efforts on a local level, it will take large-scale action to meaningfully slow climate change.

"We are at the frontline and getting hit by [Mother Nature's] fury. That gets me very upset; it makes my blood boil," he says.

"If the world stops burning fossil fuels and reduces the emissions down to 1.5C, then they will contribute to [saving] an ancient race."

In September 2026, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) released a report warning that global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5C, exceeding global targets .

"You know it's not just an island for us. It's not just our home," Mosby says.

This island is our school. This island is our maternity ward. This island is our science lab. This island is our library.

He warns that climate change drives culture into extinction.

"Masig has a nickname within the Torres Strait. They call this island the teardrop of the Straits. When you leave this island, you shed tears."

Yessie Mosby's community is on the front line of climate change. He wants to see stronger action worldwide. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Although it is hard to estimate the exact rate of erosion, Masig's distinctive tip is shrinking, slowly being blurred by rising tides.

We know that this island is hurt. She is seeking help

"Already we've got traditional methods of trying to save these islands, but it has to take a village. It has to take everybody to pull as one to try and save these islands."

title: The baby in this photo isn't the story. What it reveals is
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

The sun is still hours from rising, but Western Australian senator Fatima Payman is already on her first coffee, getting ready for another day of work — and caring for a newborn.

It could be 2am or 3am. She isn't sure anymore. These days, she says time is more of a concept than a clock.

The independent senator isn't just working to an east coast time zone from Perth; she's working around the unpredictable schedule of a new mum.

"Some days it is really tough, and there are some really good days," Payman tells SBS News during an interview in Perth.

I think overall my perspective has shifted in realising how tough women have it out there.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Payman is the first WA senator to have a baby while serving in parliament — a distinction that comes with its own challenges, including the more than 3,600km distance between Perth and Canberra.

Between herself and her husband, Jacob Stokes, a former WA Labor staffer, Payman says they are juggling the demands of parenthood with support from their respective families in Perth.

Fatima Payman is the first WA senator to have a baby while serving in parliament. Source: SBS News / Christopher Tan

Their daughter, Aliyah, was born in May this year, the couple's first child, and the family spent the first four months in Perth before Payman returned to Canberra to work earlier this month.

Payman's experience highlights a question that goes beyond one senator: As more women enter politics, has parliament changed enough to accommodate the realities of having a family?

The challenge of motherhood in parliament

Payman's working day now unfolds around the needs of a newborn, with the routines of motherhood squeezed between emails, meetings and the demands of parliamentary work.

There are feeds, nappy changes and playtime, followed by putting Aliyah to sleep and expressing breast milk to ensure there is enough for the day.

In between, Payman reads emails, keeps up to date with political developments and attends virtual meetings.

Fatima Payman says becoming a mother has given her a deeper appreciation of the challenges women face in balancing work and parenthood. Source: SBS News / Christopher Tan

By the afternoon, she is often driving to community meetings and other events, sometimes with Aliyah in the baby seat, before returning home for the evening routine.

"I am incredibly blessed to have a supportive family around me.

"As they say, it takes a village to raise a baby."

After Aliyah was born, Payman says she did not take an extended break from work.

"I didn't have a maternity leave; it was really right back to work as soon as I could, answering calls," she says.

As an independent senator, Payman's circumstances differ from those of senators in larger political parties, where responsibilities can be shared among multiple members.

Fatima Payman resigned from the Labor Party in July 2024 and went on to launch her own political party, Australia's Voice, in October 2024. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

She became an independent after crossing the floor in June 2024 to support a motion recognising Palestinian statehood. She resigned from the Labor Party the following month and, in October 2024, launched her own political party, Australia's Voice.

Payman is currently the only senator representing Australia's Voice.

"I had various Labor backbench senators reach out, some have even sent me gifts which are really lovely," she says.

"They told me they would be able to take three to four months of complete maternity leave, and that's a luxury not afforded to independent senators."

A parliament adapting to parenting

Payman's experience comes after years of scrutiny of the parliamentary workplaces and whether they are equipped to accommodate people with caring responsibilities.

In 2021, hundreds of people were interviewed as part of Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins' Set the Standard review into the culture of Commonwealth parliamentary workplaces. Their testimony highlighted power imbalances, gender inequality, a lack of accountability, entitlement and exclusion as contributing to a toxic workplace culture.

The review also identified parliament's long and irregular sitting hours as a factor affecting the well-being of people working there, and made 28 recommendations aimed at creating safer, more diverse and inclusive workplaces.

A 2022 report by UNSW Sydney and the Pathways to Politics Program for Women examined the barriers facing parliamentarians with caring responsibilities, noting that women continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of unpaid care work.

The report warned that if parliament could not reconcile caring responsibilities with its democratic duties, women could be discouraged from entering politics or remaining in parliament long-term.

It proposed five changes to make parliament more "care-friendly", including changes to sitting hours and the parliamentary calendar, formal parental leave for politicians, greater access to childcare and more use of virtual proceedings.

The report also recommended changing rules that classified children as "strangers" and did not permit them in parliamentary chambers.

Some of those changes are now visible inside parliament, from childcare facilities to the rules governing babies in the chambers.

Parliament House has an onsite childcare centre, as well as parents' rooms and facilities for nursing and infant care. The building is also accredited as a Breastfeeding Friendly Workplace.

Senators can breastfeed an infant in the chamber and, at the discretion of the Senate president, briefly care for an infant during proceedings, provided the business of the Senate is not disrupted.

That shift came into focus in 2017, when Greens senator Larissa Waters — now the party's federal leader — brought her baby into the Senate chamber to breastfeed during a sitting.

A turning point for parents in parliament

For Waters, bringing her baby into the chamber exposed a simple mismatch between parliamentary rules and the realities of being a new parent.

"I think all workplaces should be flexible and support new parents. Not just mum[s], but dads should get that flexibility," Waters tells SBS News.

Australian Greens senator Larissa Waters moved a motion on black lung disease while breastfeeding her daughter in the Senate chamber in 2017. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

Discussing the watershed moment in 2017, Waters says she was not thinking about making history when she breastfed her daughter during a sitting. Her partner texted her that their daughter was hungry and couldn't wait another five minutes, so she brought her into the chamber to feed her.

"To be honest, I wasn't thinking about the moment it would become; I was just thinking bubba was hungry and I still had to move a motion about preventing black lung disease in Queensland coal mine workers," she says.

Since then, babies have been brought into both the Senate and House of Representatives, including by male politicians. In 2024, Victorian senator Raff Ciccone became the first father to bring a baby into the chamber.

"That modelling of shared care is so important because we know dads only take about 20 per cent of the [primary] parental leave they are entitled to take," Waters says.

"And unless you start that good quality relationship and you share that care from day one, you end up with the mum doing all the work."

Waters says she was able to balance caring for her daughter with her parliamentary responsibilities.

I am a politician and I am a mum, I am both things at all times.

Has female representation changed parliament?

Sue Williamson, an associate professor at UNSW who specialises in areas of gender equality in the workplace, says federal Labor's push to increase the number of women in parliament does not necessarily mean the institution is gender-equal.

"There has been an increase in numbers of women in parliament over the past few years, particularly since the Albanese government got in," she tells SBS News.

Sue Williamson, an associate professor at UNSW who specialises in workplace gender equality, says Labor's efforts to boost female representation in parliament do not necessarily make parliament itself a gender-equal institution. Source: Supplied / Alexandra Orme

"Women now make up almost 50 per cent of parliamentarians, but gender inequalities still exist."

Williamson says gender equality depends not just on who is represented in parliament, but on workplace culture and whether people can balance political careers with caring responsibilities.

Gender equality is more about having equal representation.

"It also goes to the culture of the workplace and we know that historically Parliament House has been a really blokey workplace."

A different challenge for an independent

For Payman, Williamson says being the sole senator representing her party puts her in a unique position, with fewer resources and colleagues to rely on for support.

"Being an independent senator means she doesn't have a lot of resources," she says.

As a new mother and the sole parliamentary representative of Australia's Voice, Fatima Payman says she has limited party resources and support to draw on as she returns to work. Source: SBS News / Christopher Tan

"Already we are hearing from her that she is using her family, her partner, and relatives to provide care for the baby, which is great [that] she has that support network, but not everyone does have that support."

Williamson says Payman's experience, still attracting attention, raises a broader question of whether parliament has changed enough to support politicians with young families.

What really struck me with this story is that, why is this a story? Why are we still talking about this in 2026?

"When male politicians have babies, it's part of life, it's business as usual because they've got someone that can look after their kid."

Waters says babies in parliament can also remind politicians who they are making decisions for.

"There is a sense of delight when there is a baby in the chamber," she says.

"It's one of those moments that really breaks down the political party lines and it is a lovely reality check because it reminds you you are here for people, and that little child's future is being decided by the decisions that you take."

Waters says while parliament has made progress, there is still a broader issue of gender inequality across Australian workplaces.

I think the culture has changed, but we still have a long way to go and more importantly, workplaces around the country have a long way to go.

title: 'Deeply offensive' to suggest farmers 'prefer to abuse and exploit backpackers', NFF says
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's peak farming body says new visa limits could leave growers short of workers during key harvest periods.

The body has rejected any suggestion that farmers rely on backpackers because Pacific workers are harder to exploit.

Australia's peak farming body has accused Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke of making "deeply offensive" comments about farmers, as concern grows over how changes to backpacker visas could affect the nation's agricultural workforce.

The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) has warned the changes could contribute to higher food prices if they leave growers without enough workers during key harvest periods — times when farmers often hire 'backpackers' on Working Holiday visas.

While Burke acknowledged the migration changes would create challenges for some, he suggested the agricultural sector could utilise additional capacity in the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.

The scheme allows eligible Australian businesses to recruit workers from nine Pacific island countries and Timor-Leste when there are not enough local workers available.

Burke also said the strengthening of protections for PALM workers during his tenure as employment minister had led to warnings from some agricultural employers that they would turn away from the PALM scheme.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"At the time that we were improving those rules, we had some of the farm organisations say to us, 'If you do this, our members will just go and use backpackers,'" Burke told SBS News.

"If the reason that people are more reliant on backpackers and refusing to use Pacific workers is because they're upset that we've ended exploitation in those areas, I think that is a very different question for a number of operators."

He also stressed the criticism did not apply to the entire agricultural sector, saying "that doesn't depict the whole of the farm sector, not for a minute".

Richard Shannon, executive officer of the NFF Horticulture Council, labelled Burke's comments as "provocative" and rejected any suggestion that employers had moved away from the PALM scheme because of stronger protections for workers.

"The minister is suggesting that employers in horticulture would prefer to abuse and exploit backpackers than remain in the PALM program," Shannon told SBS News.

"This is not about exploiting people and finding loopholes, and it's deeply offensive."

Shannon argued that the reason some employers had moved away from PALM was because changes to the scheme had increased costs and administrative requirements.

He said backpackers and PALM workers also served different purposes within the agricultural workforce and could not simply be substituted for one another.

Employers in the PALM scheme have responsibilities including arranging accommodation and transport and providing additional support to workers.

Shannon said those requirements made the scheme significantly more expensive for employers than hiring backpackers, particularly for businesses needing workers for shorter periods.

The changes come as parts of Australia's horticulture industry approach major summer harvest periods, when growers can require large numbers of workers for relatively short periods.

"What [Burke] is effectively doing now is shortening the supply of backpackers and pushing people, employers, back into a program that is uncommercial for them," he said.

Why are farmers concerned about the visa changes?

Under the federal government's migration overhaul announced on Thursday, working holidaymakers wanting to remain in Australia for a second or third year will have to enter a ballot after completing the required regional work.

Second-year places will be capped at 45,000, compared with 57,000 people who qualified last year, while third-year places will fall from 31,000 to 5,000.

The government says the changes will give it greater control over migration numbers while retaining incentives for backpackers to work in regional Australia.

The government has also announced agriculture will receive priority under changes to skilled visa processing.

Shannon said the agricultural sector's immediate reaction to the changes has been "alarm", and farmers were seeking more detail from the government about how the changes would affect workforce availability.

"We have no detail as to what effect this might have on the workforce that's available in the short term and ongoing," he said.

"That's so important for our growers right now — to better understand what effect this is going to have on the numbers of backpackers in the region, and whether or not they need to make alternative plans."

Shannon also said any significant shortage of workers could ultimately flow through to consumers through higher production costs.

"It's quite clear that there's going to be a shortage now of workers, and that prices of food are going to go up."

Shannon said agricultural worker shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic had also led to such price rises but added that the industry was still uncertain about exactly how Labor's changes would affect worker availability during key harvest periods.

The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences reported in late 2021 that fruit and vegetable prices had risen above their usual seasonal levels but said declining availability of overseas agricultural workers was only one possible cause.

What's happening to Working Holiday visas?

The government's recently announced changes form part of a broader effort to bring net overseas migration down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.

Burke said working holidaymakers accounted for 48,000 places in the nation's net overseas migration figure last year, arguing no part of the visa system could be excluded from efforts to reduce overall numbers.

Backpackers will still need to complete 88 days of specified regional work to qualify for a second year and six months to qualify for a third.

But completing that work will no longer guarantee an additional year. Eligible applicants will instead enter the new ballots for the limited number of places.

At the same time, the government says processing of primary working holidaymaker applications will return to faster rates for countries whose visa arrangements include the regional work requirement.

Shannon said the NFF wanted the government to leave the existing working holidaymaker arrangements in place rather than impose the new caps.

title: Albanese begins internet safety, Security Council push in the United States

Anthony Albanese has arrived in California ahead of talks with tech giant Apple and an online safety push at the United Nations.

The prime minister landed in San Jose on Saturday morning AEST, for the first part of a week-long visit to the United States and was greeted by Australian ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty

Planning a trip overseas soon? Be prepared to pay more to fly

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) warned this week that airfares will continue to climb as oil prices bounce higher and the war in the Middle East drags on.

In its Domestic Airline Competition in Australia report, it also revealed just how concentrated the market is locally.

Qantas Group, which also owns Jetstar, dominates with a 65.2 per cent share, Virgin Australia 33.3 per cent and Rex just 1.5 per cent.

"We'll be watching closely," ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gotlieb told me on the SBS On the Money podcast.

"We want to make sure they keep independently setting prices and independently make commercial decisions despite these challenging conditions."

Cass-Gotlieb said that while airlines may navigate higher jet fuel prices by cutting capacity, which means fewer seats in the sky, relief might come in time as Sydney's second airport comes online.

"What Western Sydney (International) will introduce is more available slots for take-off and landings and that can assist with new entrant airlines which we are hoping to see."

The Western Sydney International Airport is scheduled to commence commercial passenger services in October.

If global central banks sneeze, will the RBA catch the same cold?

Well, the reality is the Reserve Bank was already lifting official interest rates earlier this year before many other global central banks, because Australia was experiencing inflationary pressures before the war in the Middle East started.

But now, global central banks have started addressing price pressures relating to higher oil prices by lifting interest rates.

Last week, the Bank of Japan boosted rates to a 31-year high, while the US Federal Reserve also moved higher for the first time in more than three years.

So while Australian interest rates don't always move in tandem, economists say the world economy is now facing the same inflationary pressures.

Investment bank UBS became the latest to change its forecast and is now expecting two more RBA rate rises this year, taking the official cash rate to 4.8 per cent, with the first to come at the next meeting at the end of this month.

It blames three things: a change in tune from global central banks which are now lifting rates; higher oil prices stemming from the war in the Middle East; and large investments in artificial intelligence.

And while higher interest rates aren't good for borrowers, it'll benefit savers depending on just how aggressive the banks are to attract deposits.

title: 'Temper tantrum': Why European countries are moving gold out of the US
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Donald Trump loves gold so much he has made it a symbol of his presidency.

Gold signage stands outside the Oval Office, gilded ornaments sit on its fireplace, and walls and ceilings now feature gold embellishments.

But while Trump may see gold as a visual shorthand for wealth and success, recent moves by France and the Netherlands to shift their gold reserves out of the United States may signal the exact opposite.

This month, the Netherlands announced it had transferred 86 tonnes of gold — equivalent to almost 7,000 bars — from vaults in the US and Canada to the Bank of England in London.

Although the transfer of around 59 tonnes of this was achieved by trading gold in New York for gold in London, more than 27 tonnes were physically moved.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The De Nederlandsche Bank said it was motivated by "increasing geopolitical unrest".

"Keeping a larger share of the gold reserves in London strengthens the function of gold as an anchor of trust," the bank said in a statement on 2 September.

US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office launching the "Trump Gold Card", a visa program that allows foreign nationals permanent residency and a pathway to US citizenship. Source: Getty / The Washington Post / Demetrius Freeman

The move follows France's announcement earlier this year that it had also shifted 129 tonnes of its gold from New York.

Some countries have been buying more gold in recent years, driving up the volume held by central banks. Between 2018 and 2025, reserves increased by 8.5 per cent.

During the same period, the price of gold has skyrocketed, increasing the market value of these reserves by 268 per cent, according to the International Monetary Fund.

Some experts say the moves could reflect concerns about the stability of institutions the world has relied on for decades.

Why do countries buy gold?

A country generally holds gold as part of its reserve assets, which act as a financial safety net. Reserves can help maintain the value of currency, protect against financial crises, and ensure countries can pay for imports and meet international debt repayments.

Australia's central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), holds 80 tonnes of gold as part of its reserve assets, alongside government bonds from other countries.

Australia stores around 6,450 gold bars in London as part of its reserve. These ABC Bullion bars made in Sydney match the standard "Good Delivery" specifications set by the London Bullion Market Association and weigh around 12.4 kilograms each. Each bar is worth about $2.4 million each, according to spot prices on 15 September. The RBA stores hold four gold bars in Australia as part of its reserve. Source: SBS News

While Australia's gold reserves have largely remained unchanged since 1997, there's been a shift among other central banks such as China, India, Poland and Türkiye, which have started to favour buying gold over US government bonds.

Poland has significantly increased its gold reserves over the last 20 years, building it up from just 14 tonnes in 1996 to more than 630 tonnes by mid-2026.

Scott French, a senior lecturer at the University of NSW's school of economics, says gold is a commodity with intrinsic value that tends to increase over time.

No-one's ever going to default on gold.

This makes it a safe asset that generally doesn't lose its value even when interest rates are high, unlike government bonds.

The disadvantage of gold, however, is that it doesn't provide any income.

"Gold just sits there and doesn't produce anything; it doesn't pay interest."

Gold v bonds

One reason US government bonds are popular among investors, beyond their status as safe assets, is that they generate regular interest income.

Bonds are issued by governments to borrow money. If you buy a bond, the country pays you a fixed interest rate (known as a coupon) and will also repay the original amount you lent (the principal) when the bond matures.

The US Treasury market is the largest government bond market in the world, and US government bonds (known as Treasuries) are considered one of the safest financial assets.

This is because the US government has a long history of meeting its debt obligations, and it can also raise money by increasing taxes if it needs to generate additional income — something that is not available to companies.

READ MORE Australian families could be sitting on a goldmine, but many are torn about selling

But if inflation and interest rates rise — as they are currently in the US — the income received in interest from the bond will be less valuable, which also makes the bond more difficult to sell.

John Hawkins, a senior lecturer at the University of Canberra, says investors tend to buy gold when they are worried about rising interest rates and government debt, which can leave countries struggling to pay back bonds.

"[Gold] is one of the few alternatives to a government bond," the former RBA economist says.

Maintaining a stockpile of gold bullion within a country's own borders also makes these physical assets harder to seize and more secure than intangible financial assets.

Hawkins says global examples of assets being frozen may have highlighted the risks of storing physical assets overseas. He points to the seizure of Russia's foreign-held assets, including money held in bank accounts, following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Why are countries moving gold out of the US?

Securing greater control over assets may have been a factor in France's decision to sell the 129 tonnes of gold it had stored in New York last financial year. The country bought back the same amount of gold based in Europe and has stored this with the rest of its reserve in a vast underground vault known as the 'Souterraine' in Paris.

This gives it direct control over 2,437 tonnes of gold, the fourth-largest gold reserve in the world after the US, Germany and Italy (excluding the International Monetary Fund).

Gold reserves at the Banque de France. Source: Getty / Sygma / Pierre Perrin

Unlike France, the Netherlands opted to move some of its US-held gold to London rather than store it domestically. Around 37 per cent of the country's reserves also remain in the US and Canada.

London is an attractive place to store gold as it's a hub where buyers and sellers can trade large volumes of the metal. It also hosts major gold storage vaults, including those linked to the Bank of England.

The London bullion market is regarded as the world's largest gold trading centre and sets the LBMA Gold Price benchmark.

"If you have gold in London, you can mobilise it more quickly, more effectively, more easily," Nicholas Frappell, the global head of institutional markets at Australia's ABC Refinery, says.

The vast majority of Australia's 80-tonne gold reserve is stored at the Bank of England.

The Bank of England controls major gold storage vaults. Source: Getty / In Pictures / Mike Kemp

An RBA spokesperson says storing its gold there gives the RBA ready access to the gold market, as most market participants prefer to take delivery in London.

"The Bank of England provides a very secure and cost-effective storage location for central banks and other market participants," they said.

While these factors may have played a part in the decisions by France and the Netherlands to move gold out of the US, Hawkins says concerns around the erratic leadership of US President Trump may have also been a motivating factor.

[Trump's] threatened all sorts of measures against European countries if they don't do what he likes.

"So they're worried that some sort of temper tantrum … might lead to him somehow seizing the gold that's held in New York that's owned by those countries."

Questions over US stability

Hawkins says countries moving gold out of the US could be interpreted as "a decrease in confidence" in the US.

"I think the impact over the last few years is basically down to people not having confidence in the stability of the US and that's basically down to Trump."

Along with gold, central banks also hold foreign currencies in their reserve assets. Data shows foreign reserves of the US dollar appear to be declining.

In 2000, the US dollar made up 71 per cent of global foreign exchange reserves held by central banks, according to Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves data.

While the US remains the world's dominant reserve currency, it now only makes up around 57 per cent of reserves.

The US dollar was backed by gold until 1971. Source: Getty / CFOTO / Future Publishing

French says confidence in financial systems is very important, as most countries now have 'fiat currencies' — a term that describes government-issued currencies not backed by gold or any other physical commodity.

It relies on the belief in stability of the government that's backing that currency, and trust in the rest of society to continue to accept that currency.

The US dollar used to be backed by gold under the Bretton Woods system, with other countries linking their currencies to the dollar. This helped establish the global trading system and gave the US dollar prominence, which endures today despite it no longer being backed by gold.

One of the reasons why the Chinese renminbi is unlikely to become a dominant reserve currency, despite China's economic strength, is due to perceived uncertainty. It currently makes up just 2 per cent of foreign currency reserves held by central banks.

While there is confidence in the Chinese government's ability to pay its bonds, French says the country's institutions are seen as beholden to the Chinese Communist Party and President Xi Jinping.

"You're putting a lot of faith in one person to act responsibly and you never know what that one person is going to do, so that makes it a riskier long-term investment," French says.

Tight political control of Chinese institutions under the leadership of President Xi Jinping makes investment more risky. Source: Getty / Evan Vucci / Pool

What happens after Trump?

For now, the US dollar remains the proverbial 'gold standard', despite lingering concerns over Trump's volatility.

The president's comments aimed at exerting control over institutions, including repeatedly attacking the Federal Reserve for not cutting interest rates, have undermined faith in the independence of US decision-making, French says.

He has also put the US on a "very precarious fiscal path" by cutting taxes last year without significantly cutting US spending, at a time when the country has a $60 trillion budget deficit, which has raised questions about its ability to repay bonds.

But French says the US Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates this week despite criticism from Trump is a positive sign of its credibility.

Ironically, one of the best things for the Trump administration … is for the central bank to do what [the president] doesn't want them to do.

French doesn't think Trump has done enough damage yet for the US dollar to be dumped as the global reserve currency.

"We're almost halfway into the second Trump administration … I wouldn't expect to see anything catastrophic over the next couple of years," he says.

"So really the question is, what happens after Donald Trump?"

French says if the next administration behaves responsibly, there's no reason the US dollar won't remain the dominant global currency for the next couple of decades.

"If further administrations continue on the same path, then we could be in trouble for multiple reasons."

title: Nearly two million Quest Apartment Hotels customers affected by data breach
text:
In brief Quest Apartment Hotels says the information of nearly two millions customers was compromised in a data breach.

The data includes credit card, passport, and Medicare numbers.

Personal information of nearly two million Quest Apartment Hotels customers has been compromised in a data breach, including credit card, passport and Medicare numbers.

Last month, the accommodation provider identified a cyberattack on a database system via a vulnerability in a third-party technology provider.

David Mansfield, the managing director of The Ascott Limited, which owns Quest Apartment Hotels, provided an update this week, saying a forensic data analysis revealed information relating to approximately 1,991,613 customers was affected.

The majority of information related to names and contacts, but also included:

Vehicle registration numbers: 225,300

Passport and/or driver licence numbers (the number only; no scanned copies of ID documents were affected): 104,268

Credit card numbers (no CVV, including expired credit cards): 297,739

Credit card numbers (with CVV, including expired credit cards): 46,727

Date of birth: 3,328

NDIS number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 271

Medicare card number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 46

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

All the information relates to records from before June 2025.

Mansfield said the company was contacting those affected directly to inform them of which category they were in, the steps they could take, and available support.

"I recognise the concern this incident has caused. On behalf of Quest, I sincerely apologise to those who have been affected," he said.

Quest said it first identified an outage on its website on 17 August, with investigation revealing "a malicious attack" had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party service provider's software.

The company is advising customers to remain alert for suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls, particularly communications requesting personal, financial or account information.

READ MORE Australian patient details exposed in GP network cyberattack

Quest said it was cooperating with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian Cyber Security Centre and Victoria Police.

Last year's Annual Cyber Threat Report warned cyberattacks were a growing problem in Australia, with financial losses, ransomware attack frequency, and the number of reported data breaches all increasing.

After a major data breach involving millions of Optus customers in 2022, the federal government overhauled privacy laws, requiring companies to destroy or actively de-identify personal information as soon as it was no longer needed.

Incident raises data concerns

Paul Watters, chief executive of Cyberstronomy, which provides cyber risk expertise, said all businesses needed to have a clear understanding of the personal data they hold and why.

"Often, this is not the case," he told SBS News.

"Quest says all of the affected information came from records dating from before June 2025. That immediately raises a governance question: for each category of information, why was it still being retained?"

He said the incident could serve as a lesson for organisations.

"Audit your data holdings. Know what you have, where it is, why you are retaining it, how long you need it, and when it should be deleted or de-identified. Data you no longer hold cannot be stolen in a breach," he said.

Belinda Barnet, a Swinburne University data privacy expert, told SBS News the latest incident raised concerns about the type of data some companies were still retaining.

"Companies like Quest don't need to retain your passport after you've actually identified yourself," she said.

"We really need to have more public discussion about how [companies are] going to destroy information that's no longer needed."

title: The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality
text:
In brief Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said "upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising".

It reaffirmed expectations that the board would hike rates again at this month's meeting.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) fears about inflation have materialised, its governor Michele Bullock says, which could force it to raise interest rates again.

Her comments during a parliamentary hearing on Friday morning reaffirmed expectations that the central bank would hike rates for a fourth time this year at its upcoming board meeting in late September.

Inflation was too high, but the key question for the RBA at that meeting would be whether the bank's three rate rises to date were enough to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time, Bullock said.

At its last meeting in August, the RBA forecast that inflation would return to the middle of its target range of 2-3 per cent by the end of 2027.

Even that was not assured, with inflation more likely to overshoot the bank's forecasts than undershoot it.

If that proved to be the case, more rate hikes might be warranted, the RBA board said at the time.

"Developments since then suggest that, although growth in the Australian economy is slowing, some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising," Bullock said on Friday.

The Middle East conflict, the AI boom, and extreme weather events have added to pressure on energy, food, and tech prices, she said.

"There is little sign of resolution in the Middle East conflict. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add directly to inflation."

The benchmark Brent crude price remained above US$104 ($146) a barrel, despite a modest sell-off in oil overnight on news that Saudi Arabia plans to bring its East-West pipeline back online in a reduced capacity following attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces.

But as businesses increasingly saw no end in sight to the war and price increases, they were growing more inclined to pass on costs to consumers, which risked making inflation more persistent, Bullock said.

After inflation came in hotter than expected in July, money markets have raised the chance for a September rate rise above 80 per cent, with two hikes fully priced in by March.

Higher-for-longer interest rates and fuel prices would hit economic growth, but that has been swamped by the AI boom, which has pushed up demand in a way the RBA did not foresee.

"Just back from the US and in addition to ... the upside risk of inflation from the Middle East, what is also very striking is how strong the AI and tech boom is and has been," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said.

"That's not just true in the US; it's true in the Asia Pacific region as well, who are of course our closest trading partners, and our forecasts for global growth have been repeatedly surprised on the upside."

Given Australia's productivity malaise, a period of slower growth was needed to bring inflation down, Bullock said.

The nation's deepening housing downturn would help take some steam out of the economy, but while prices have fallen in most capital cities, they remain about 50 per cent higher than in early 2020.

title: Five assaulted, bottles thrown at umpires as ugly scenes erupt at tense prelim final

Football fans who threw cans and bottles at umpires face a five-year AFL ban after ugly behaviour boiled over at a tense preliminary final on Saturday night. Police fined five fans, including one who threw an item, and said five other fans were assaulted at the MCG during Brisbane’s nine-point preliminary final victory over Hawthorn. Loading Dozens of fans flung bottles and cans at the umpires as they walked off the ground after the match. Hawks fans also booed the umpires and vented their frustration over a series of high-stakes decisions in the match’s dying minutes that went the Lions’ way. Footage showed one field umpire, Jacob Mollison, reacting quickly to protect his colleague from a projectile that appeared to have been thrown from the top level of the stadium.
