Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Three contentious free kicks, one crazy minute: The detailed verdict on preliminary final umpiring calls On Sunday afternoon, police confirmed that they fined a 40-year-old from Croydon $418 for throwing a bottle, although this was not the fan who Mollison pointed out. Police said they were pleased overall with the crowd of nearly 98,000, but 10 people were evicted from the venue. Two fans were removed for “behaviour incidents” and one for entering without a ticket. “Two men were assaulted as they made their way to leave the venue. The victims were allegedly punched after remonstrating with another spectator,” police said. Another two people told police they were also punched as they were leaving, and a fifth man struck his head on a wall after an alleged push. He was not seriously injured.

In yet another incident, a mother claimed a man threw nachos at her and her son. “It’s absolutely disgusting, and I’m just sick of going out in Melbourne and being worried for my safety,” she told 3AW. Meanwhile, the AFL said in a statement: “The AFL and MCC security will work with Vic Pol to identify the bottle throwers directed at the umpires last night. If identified, they will be banned from games and the stadium for a minimum of five years.” Cans litter the ground after Hawthorn’s loss to Brisbane. Getty Images Premier Ben Carroll joined the AFL Umpires Association, the Hawks and Jeff Kennett in condemning the ugly scenes that threatened to overshadow perhaps one of the greatest football games this century. Carroll said the throwing of bottles was “not the Victorian way”.

Advertisement

“I think these people should be made an example of. This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head,” Carroll said. “You’ve always got to respect the umpire’s decision.” Former grand final umpire Ray Chamberlain said fans who threw projectiles onto the field should not come back to the football. Umpires dodge projectiles as they exit the ground. AFL Photos via Getty Images The Lions clawed back the lead moments before the final siren when Hawks defender Jarman Impey was pinged for holding the ball and Lion Hugh McCluggage coolly slotted a goal from the resultant free kick. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said he understood the fans’ emotions, but added that “we shouldn’t be throwing things on the field”.

“The emotion of sport, it’s why we love it so much,” he said in his post-match press conference. “All sports, but ours in particular – the beauty is the emotion it makes you feel. At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears. Part of me wanted to scream with rage. Part of me wanted to throw chairs.” Chamberlain, who was at the ground commentating for the ABC, also acknowledged the passion of fans, but told this masthead on Sunday that throwing bottles and cans on the arena crossed the line. “I love the passion. It is the best game in the world with 100,000 at the MCG doing its thing, but if you are going to throw stuff, don’t come back,” Chamberlain said. “Have your feelings, have an opinion, be passionate, it is what makes it great. The fans are the single most important ingredient in the whole thing. But if you are going to throw projectiles, don’t come.”

Advertisement

Mitchell was also gently critical of the umpires, saying the Impey decision was not the main one that concerned him. “[There were] a couple leading up to it and other key moments in the game. I’m sure the umpires will assess how they performed in the game in key moments.” Loading Carroll would not be drawn when asked if these comments were appropriate so soon after the ugly crowd reaction. “I thought the umpires did an excellent job, but I don’t think at any level of any sport, umpires can be having projectiles thrown at them because it is just so dangerous.”

Ex-premier and Hawks president Jeff Kennett was at the game, but said he didn’t notice any bottles being thrown as he left on the final siren. He said he saw nothing wrong with Mitchell’s comments. “I didn’t feel it was anything else but measured. You could feel the pain in it: often people give their best speeches when they lose,” he said. “Any throwing of projectiles, whatever they are, in whatever setting, is simply unacceptable.” Cans and bottles on the ground at the MCG. Getty Images AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said on Sunday that he was stunned by the spectacle. “It wasn’t just one or two or five people. It looked like it was a few hundred people around the entire ground throwing stuff onto the ground. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing,” he told this masthead.

Related Article AFL grand final Blood and tears spilled as Lions newcomer rides emotions of pulsating ‘prelim’ In a statement, AFL Umpires Association boss Rob Kerr said the actions of sections of the crowd after the siren were completely unacceptable, and welcomed the swift condemnation. “Umpiring finals football is an enormous responsibility, and the umpires met that challenge with skill and composure throughout an intensely contested match. There is no justification – ever – for responding to an umpiring decision with threatening behaviour,” Kerr said. “The umpires showed real courage to make the decisions they did in an incredibly fierce contest, executing their roles under intense pressure. For a section of the crowd to respond to a decision – made in real time – by throwing bottles at the umpires is indefensible.” Hawks fan boo the final result. via Getty Images

Earlier this year, Hawks star Nick Watson claimed he had a Coke bottle thrown at him in a match against Sydney, while a fan who threw a lemon at Eagles player Reuben Ginbey was banned for five years. Issko said the incident would be on the agenda of his group’s next meeting with the AFL, but he was unsure how to prevent a recurrence of such widespread delinquency. title: The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days
text:

Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days Dan Walsh September 20, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With a step back against the grain, a shimmy and then a pivot around yet another hapless opponent, Daly Cherry-Evans did what he does best. He finished with a grin, and a giggle, too. Sharks fullback Will Kennedy had been left for dead more than an hour earlier when the 37-year-old masterminded the Roosters’ passage to Friday’s preliminary final date with the Dolphins. Daly Cherry-Evans: Now a Rooster, once a Redcliffe Dolphins junior. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac The gaggle of reporters, slow-footed at the best of times, never stood a chance, asking about the storyline that will now loom all week next to the one regarding star halfback Sam Walker’s rapidly healed ankle ligaments. Especially considering Cherry-Evans’ tripping charge against Teig Wilton ended as expected on Sunday with a $1000 fine from the match review committee.

Advertisement

But surely, Daly, you can appreciate the narrative, the rugby league romanticism of one last outing at a sold-out Suncorp Stadium? Against the Redcliffe-based Dolphins no less, where he took those first furtive steps in rugby league as a six-year-old for Redcliffe more than 30 years ago, where his dad and uncle both played as well? “I completely understand the sentiment, but they are just storylines,” Cherry-Evans said with a smile when his links to the Dolphins were raised. “At the end of the day, we’re playing a prelim … At no stage have we made it about me or anyone who is leaving the club. Because while those things create great headlines, they distract us from what we need to do here, which is play footy.” Loading Cherry-Evans, throughout an enthralling 16-year, 377-game career (which pushes well past 400 appearances when 21 Tests and 26 Origins are included), often inadvertently, so often has. Few have provided such regular, meaty copy.

Advertisement

And as for the Redcliffe connections, the 30-year-old archived photos do more justice than words ever could. In more recent times, the Dolphins have eyed off that cherub-cheeked kid more than once as a potential star signing. In 2021, when he still could, Manly owner Scott Penn issued a “hands off” edict as Redcliffe hunted culture-setting marquee signings while establishing their first NRL roster. When things fell apart between the Sea Eagles and Cherry-Evans, the Dolphins were one of the few clubs the veteran No.7 actually met with and weighed up as an option, though the Roosters were always early clubhouse leaders for his signature. A young Daly Cherry-Evans (fourth from right) with his father, Troy (red jacket, back row) in 1996. Now, after more than 33,000 minutes of top-level rugby league (80 x 424 games, you can work out all the extra time), Cherry-Evans now has just either 80 or 160 minutes left in the NRL.

Advertisement

By his own admission, he was sub-par against Penrith in the Roosters’ 19-12 week one finals loss. No one has slotted more field goals than Cherry-Evans’ 31 in the NRL era. But the late attempt he shanked – by his lofty standards, oh so badly – was, according to Fox Sports stats, the 50th missed one-pointer of his career, too. It doesn’t matter in the wash of a truly glittering career. Except for the explanation Cherry-Evans offers after getting back to his best against Cronulla, with that crucial 27th minute solo try and three try assists as well. “You won’t find anyone harder on my own game than myself. It’s as simple as that,” he said after being the last Rooster to emerge from Allianz Stadium. “But what happens next is if I carry my divots, I’m then not only putting myself out, but my team out [too]. From the words of the great Ted Lasso, memory of a goldfish.”

Advertisement

That selective memory – “sporting amnesia” as Trent Robinson dubbed it on Saturday night – was perfect for jettisoning the attacking missteps against Penrith. Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Confident’: Walker eyes remarkable return as DCE sets up storybook Dolphins clash Less so, the way the Dolphins pulled his right-side defensive combination with Rob Toia apart in their last clash. In a 26-12 victory for the Queenslanders, one that announced their arrival as proper premiership contenders, they went after Cherry-Evans and no doubt plan to do so again on Friday night. The Roosters’ right edge has been a work in progress all season. Halves are naturally targeted; Cherry-Evans as much as any. Yet, while the Roosters scored eight tries to Cronulla’s two at Allianz Stadium, the Sharks weren’t able to exploit the veteran No.7, despite having more tackles (38-27) inside the opposition 20-metre zone. “Defence wins you competitions there’s no doubt about it,” Cherry-Evans said.

“Last week [against Penrith], while we didn’t get the win, for the most part of the game it was a really great defensive effort. And we leaned on that [against the Sharks] again, didn’t we? “The try line defence, when we needed to, more often than not, we turned them away. If we continue to do that, we can really grow as a side.”

title: Activist group using AI to flood ABC with thousands of bias complaints
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive BusinessCompaniesMiddle East tensions Activist group using AI to flood ABC with thousands of bias complaints Calum Jaspan September 20, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Activist groups are using artificial intelligence to target the ABC’s coverage of the Middle East with accusations of bias, contributing to a sharp rise in the number of coordinated complaints detected by the public broadcaster’s independent ombudsman. One of those groups is Pen Power Australia, which has been using AI technology to coordinate complaints to the ABC’s board and management to attempt to correct what it sees as bias and make coverage more favourable to Israel. Institutions such as the ABC are grappling with large numbers of complaints that activist groups are coordinating through tech platforms. Sam Mooy A new report released by the ABC’s Ombudsman on Thursday found that organised complaint campaigns rose sharply over the past year, in part due to the assistance of artificial intelligence. The report did not name Pen Power, but ABC ombudsman Fiona Cameron identified 48 “campaigns” during the year ending June 30 which accounted for 5259 total complaints, or 61 per cent of all content complaints received.

Advertisement

“Complaints were categorised as campaigns where a concentration of complaints raised similar concerns about the same content within a specific period. They may be substantively similar or identically worded or appear coordinated,” the ombudsman’s report notes. The report underscores how coordinated campaigns are making it more difficult for organisations like the ABC to gauge the level of community anger over hot-button issues such as the Middle East as they seek to balance genuine engagement with resisting pressure campaigns. Pen Power’s coordinator John Grimwade said the campaigns he had organised could have anything from 100 people to a few thousand sending complaint letters if he could enlist support from overseas groups. The group runs campaigns about Gaza, Israel and anything connected to these issues, he said. Last month, Grimwade told the group its members had sent more than 40,000 letters by email to date, according to internal WhatsApp messages seen by this masthead. “Our campaigns go out as required,” Grimwade said. “We try to keep up with the ABC in particular but so many of their reports are biased or statements made that lack proper context.”

Advertisement

Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu’s rivals call him ‘unfit’ for office after report he was warned of October 7 attack In March, ABC chair Kim Williams defended the broadcaster against accusations of bias, saying it stood by its coverage of the conflict in the Middle East. Grimwade, an Adelaide retiree, confirmed the group has used a platform called Activist Mailer, which boasts online of letting users coordinate campaigns with artificial intelligence. The platform’s website claims that its platform makes what would otherwise appear as a barrage of emails appear “unique” by using different words, tone, formating and length to deliver the same coordinated message, “each sent directly from supporters’ own inboxes”. “The result? Messages that get read, voices that get heard, and movements that drive real change.”

Advertisement

But Grimwade is planning on changing to a new AI platform. “I am currently using the Activist Mailer but will be changing most of our campaigns over to the new AI,” Grimwade said. Letter-writing campaigns have worked in the past. In late 2023, the ABC sacked casual radio host Antoinette Lattouf after a coordinated letter-writing campaign targeted members of the broadcaster’s board and management team, including then-chair Ita Buttrose. That campaign was driven by a separate pro-Israel group and did not include Pen Power Australia. A Federal Court judge last year found the ABC had sacked Lattouf unlawfully and she was awarded $150,000 in damages. The case cost the ABC more than $2 million. Grimwade said his campaigns had had little success so far beyond yielding a response from ABC head of editorial standards Gavin Fang or the ombudsman. “In simple terms, they think they are right,” he said. But he said Pen Power had succeeded in getting an Instagram video removed in recent days featuring Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran covering the Iran war.

Advertisement

“We have had a video on Instagram taken down, which we are claiming as a win,” Grimwade said. “It was removed shortly after our letters were starting to be sent.” Related Article Media & marketing ABC slams watchdog finding that Four Corners program failed impartiality test In a statement, an ABC spokesperson said the video had already been taken down before the first campaign email came in because the reporter misread the script, resulting in an error. “In any event, the campaign would have been immaterial because when we identify errors, we always take action,” the spokesperson said. In a podcast interview with the conservative Australian Jewish Association, Grimwade claimed his campaigns had more success outside the ABC. Pen Power last week organised a campaign of emails to the ABC managing director Hugh Marks, chair Kim Williams and Fang, claiming the ABC’s reporting on Israel-Palestine was inaccurate and not impartial.

Advertisement

“As long as it’s antisemitic, we’ll have a go,” Grimwade told AJA chief executive Robert Gregory. Gregory praised Grimwade and thanked him “for the work you’re doing”. The two organisations have a “limited” partnership, Grimwade confirmed. In another call-out this week, Pen Power produced a letter asking members to target the ABC over its Middle Eastern guidance document. “Please join with us and send the letter exposing it for what it really is. Another ABC document that is bias [sic] and factually incorrect,” the message said. It isn’t just Australian groups pushing these coordinated campaigns, Grimwade said. “I am aware of overseas groups doing the same as us and we sometimes use each other’s letters where it’s applicable to do so,” he said, without naming his international allies. “The only other Australian group is a WhatsApp chat group that was formed specifically to tackle the ABC problem.” The ombudsman said 1148 (13 per cent of all content complaints) related to the Israel-Palestine conflict. The volume of allegations of both pro-Israel or pro-Palestine coverage were about equal, the report said.

Advertisement

But allegations of pro-Iranian coverage topped both allegations of pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian coverage. The US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. The ABC received 2746 complaints from across the globe about an Instagram reel published in May, focusing on its reporting from inside Iran. Most complaints were made by “Iranian Australians” or “Iranians in the diaspora community” the ombudsman said, and alleged the post lacked impartiality. The ombudsman also noted “68 identical complaints by email to the ABC board and other recipients (rather than the ABC complaints form)” regarding an April episode of Radio National program If You’re Listening about the war in Iran. The identical complaints said the episode presented Iran as a “reasonable diplomatic partner” and Israel as an “antagonist” and “disruptor of diplomacy”, suggesting a lack of impartiality, the ombudsman’s report, which cleared the piece of content of any breaches, said. The ombudsman has since changed its classification of complaints it identifies as identical or coordinated, counting them as one complaint. This masthead is not suggesting this complaint was organised by Pen Power. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: Albo wanders in to Tim Apple’s place to fix the internet

Analysis PoliticsFederalSocial media Albo wanders in to Tim Apple’s place to fix the internet Rob Harris September 20, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was something almost The Truman Show about Anthony Albanese’s Californian morning at Apple Park. The prime minister had travelled to the heart of Silicon Valley to meet Tim Cook – or, as Donald Trump once called him, “Tim Apple” – and spruik Australia’s world-leading crackdown on social media for under-16s. The prime minister gets a demonstration of Apple’s new child safety features at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer If only Ed Harris had wandered into shot to tell him the whole thing was a set. Instead, there was the enormous circular Apple “Spaceship” headquarters with its carbon-sink oak forest across 70 hectares, with olive groves, roaming coyotes, gleaming glass and enough security to ensure the travelling journalists saw only the parts of the $5 billon compound that Apple wanted them to see.

Advertisement

The media pack was briefly allowed inside the foyer for a child-friendly product demonstration of Apple’s latest products, including the new foldable Duo phone. It’s just $3499. But the meeting was off limits. No cameras nor photographs, not even pictures of the buildings or Apple employees. The journalists could look, but they could not record. Not even a sighting of the cult leader. Welcome to the world of “Tim Apple”, complete with the Steve Jobs Memorial Theatre. Albanese spent an hour behind closed doors with Cook and the Apple executive team, continuing a relationship that began when the Apple boss called him in June to discuss the company’s new child-safety controls. Cook had told Albanese the changes were partly inspired by Australia’s world-leading social media age ban, as well as Apple’s own research into the effects of social media on children.

Now the bromance was rekindled at Apple Park. Tech brothers from another mother. Apple executive chairman Tim Cook with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese on x.com Cook later posted that he was grateful to welcome @AlboMP to Apple Park to discuss the company’s “longstanding commitment to Australia” and its latest innovations to help keep children safe online. Albanese, who rarely meets a celebrity without an obligatory for a selfie, was even more effusive. He said it was a “proud moment” to have the head of a company that had “changed the world” recognise Australia’s leadership in protecting children from the negative consequences of technology.

Related Article Updated

AI Albanese urges US, China to strike AI deal akin to nuclear non-proliferation treaty Apple’s new controls allow parents to limit the time children spend on particular apps and devices, restrict who can message them and introduce other safeguards. There was, however, a rather obvious irony hanging over the morning. As one wag in the journalist pack observed that the scene was a bit like McDonald’s selling shots of Ozempic as part of a meal deal. Apple is, after all, one of the companies most responsible for putting a powerful computer in the pockets of just about every adult – and an increasingly large number of children. Albanese was at pains to say this was not a war on technology.

Advertisement

The iPhone and Apple’s products had delivered “enormous benefits”, he said, while artificial intelligence could improve healthcare, including cancer detection and diagnosis. The task, in the prime minister’s telling, was to make sure people remained in control. View post on X That argument will be central to Albanese’s international push on artificial intelligence as he prepares for talks at the United Nations. He also discussed the government’s proposed “My Feed, My Way” reforms, which would give users greater control over the algorithms to determine what appears in their social media feeds.

Advertisement

Embattled developer Bathla Group was slapped with more than 300 notices by SafeWork NSW relating to safety issues in the five years leading up to its collapse. Janie Barrett “The five most common notices were related to falls from heights, electrical hazards, construction site security, general workplace management and falling objects,” a SafeWork NSW spokesperson said. “SafeWork NSW continues to work with the business to monitor its progress in taking any required compliance actions.”

It’s been a difficult few weeks for the major developer and its 542 entities, which entered voluntary administration on August 25. title: Three contentious free kicks, one crazy minute: The detailed verdict on preliminary final umpiring calls
text:
Advertisement

Loading

The skills of the players in this intense, classic preliminary final between Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions were the real highlight but when three free kicks are paid in the final 61 seconds and the lead changes those umpiring decisions will be examined and reviewed in fine detail. Football writers Peter Ryan, Marc McGowan and former AFL grand final umpire “Razor” Ray Chamberlain took a close look at the final three free kicks to the Brisbane Lions and whether they were justified. 1. Lewis shows insufficient intent (62 seconds remaining) Peter Ryan says: The only query is whether a free kick would be paid in the first minute of a game, but beyond that, there is no doubt it was a free kick. The AFL clarified the rule after round two this season in a memo to clubs, which basically said a token effort to touch the ball before it went out of bounds would be insufficient intent. Mitch Lewis would have got away with it if he’d either grabbed the ball and momentum took him out or made a genuine attempt to keep the ball in play (which is difficult as he would have risked missing the ball). It’s a fair call. And remember Lewis hardly fumbled all match. His response to the decision was very professional.

Advertisement

Marc McGowan says: Lewis wasn’t trying to keep the ball in play. AFL headquarters made it clear early in the season that simply attempting to touch the ball to avoid a “lasso” free kick would no longer suffice, so as harsh as this seems, the umpire made the correct call. Ray Chamberlain says: The action of Lewis is all that matters when it comes to insufficient intent, but for context, Jack Ginnivan kicks an end-over-end grubber along the boundary line. If it goes out of bounds without being touched it is a last-disposal free kick. Lewis has to show sufficient intent to keep the ball in play. Has the Lewis’ action demonstrated sufficient intent to keep the ball in play? No. The umpire made the correct call. 2. Zorko cops high contact (53 seconds remaining)

Advertisement

Peter Ryan says: Tiggy touch wood, but high contact was made and many of those are paid or not paid during a season depending on what the umpire sees. Josh Weddle’s arms made contact with Dayne Zorko above the shoulder, so it is a free kick. Marc McGowan says: Glancing blow or not, it is crystal clear that Josh Weddle made high contact to Dayne Zorko while coming from the opposite direction as the veteran Lion spun around. Would there be any controversy if Zorko had done this to Weddle? Ray Chamberlain says: There is certainly high contact. He is not decapitated by any stretch, but you can’t make high contact. He has flicked him across the face. It is going to get paid. Impey caught holding the ball

Advertisement

Peter Ryan says: Great decision by the umpire. When Jarman Impey takes possession of the ball, he has both arms free momentarily. It gives him a second where he could have handballed or kicked the ball, but he decided to do neither. Hugh McCluggage’s tackle was outstanding for the situation. After holding Impey for about a second around the waist, he then latched on to his hand, so the Hawks’ defender couldn’t handball either, making kicking Impey’s only option. The Hawk just froze and hoped the umpire would not be brave enough to pay holding the ball. Four seconds lapsed between taking possession and the decision being made. Marc McGowan says: Hugh McCluggage was brilliant, and Jarman Impey was not. The umpire was equally good. You can also effectively forget whether Impey had an initial opportunity with both arms available. McCluggage executed a tackle as players are taught – pin one arm, and remove half the options. In this scenario, Impey needed to be saved by a third party instantly coming in, or he had to attempt to get a kick away far earlier than he did. The risk was he would drop the ball and not get a foot to it, but Impey’s feigned efforts to dispose the ball were never going to be enough. Brave call, and right call. Ray Chamberlain says: The law has to line up before any decision is made with the umpire correctly assessing there was no prior opportunity, a legal tackle had been laid and the ball had not been pinned. But then there is what I call “a cadence piece” which is a question of how long do you give the player [to dispose of the ball]. If it is pinned and he can’t dispose of the ball or he is unable to make a genuine attempt, then you can call for a ball up, but if not, as is the case here, then it is free kick against Impey for holding the ball. Bravo to the umpire.

Advertisement

And for the record ... Not only were all three free kicks above the correct decisions, but Hawthorn were fortunate with non-calls on the Jacks, Ginnivan and Gunston, in the dying minutes. Mitch Lewis’ forward-50 hanger with three-and-a-half minutes to go, which would have gone down in club folklore if they won, followed Gunston shoving Harris Andrews in the back, forcefully enough that he could not contest the ball.

Advertisement

The other damning factor? Gunston’s arms were extended as he did it, so he was lucky not to cost Lewis his brilliant mark. There was another with about two-and-a-half minutes left. After Harry Morrison’s shocking turnover to Zac Bailey, which was a clear mark, Ginnivan wrenched the ball off Bailey then handballed over his head.

title: Blood and tears spilled as Lions newcomer rides emotions of pulsating ‘prelim’
text:

SportAFLAFL grand final Blood and tears spilled as Lions newcomer rides emotions of pulsating ‘prelim’ Danny Russell September 20, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As Hawthorn snatched the lead in a pulsating final three minutes of a preliminary final for the ages, Oscar Allen accepted his brave move across the country 12 months earlier had fallen a week short of his dream. Interchange rotations had reduced the powerful forward to a late-game spectator, removed from the frantic action and unable to influence the outcome from the sidelines as a trickle of blood rolled down his cheek from a gash beside his left eye. Oscar Allen leaves the field under the blood rule during Brisbane’s preliminary final win over Hawthorn. AFL Photos via Getty Images “I was on the bench at the end, and probably during the last couple of minutes when we went down, I was thinking about everything,” he told this masthead. “I was thinking about things we could have done better, things I could have done better. I was thinking about the (coming) off-season, you know, your head goes everywhere.

Advertisement

“And then, yeah, you flip to next week.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘Whatever you paid, it was worth it’: The agony and the ecstasy of the game of the season The flip to next week will go down in footy folklore – a holding-the-ball decision paid against Hawthorn defender Jarman Impey in the final minute that allowed Hugh McCluggage to kick the match-winning goal. The decisive moment sent the baying Hawthorn crowd into meltdown and the umpires were loudly, and unfairly, booed as they left the ground. But there was no such angst in the raucous Lions rooms after the match. There was sheer joy and relief. They had been to grand final in the previous three years, but this one felt harder fought, harder earned.

Advertisement

Spent-looking skipper Harris Andrews labelled the breathtaking aftermath a “serious” emotional high, beaming teammate Jarrod Berry kept saying “crazy” about his best mate McCluggage’s ability to kick two late clutch goals, while Conor McKenna said he felt grateful after a “wild last two minutes” to be back in a grand final. The Irishman also acknowledged his part in a match filled with exhilarating highs, a skilful two-touch soccer goal while dancing through congestion.“I play a bit of soccer, so it is something I can do,” he smiled. Conor McKenna celebrates his soccer goal against Hawthorn. AFL Photos via Getty Images For Allen, there were no such highs. He played a bit-part to the dynamic Kai Lohmann’s five-goal heroics, or watched in awe as Charlie Cameron did Charlie Cameron things. Not that the 27-year-old blond forward minded. He said it was simply great to be a part of something special.

Advertisement

Nor did he feel a sense of vindication for handing in the Eagles captaincy last year, amid ongoing media speculation, and departing his native Western Australia for Brisbane. Instead, he said, the move had provided its own rewards. Loading “Even without the on-field team success, like the way they made me feel welcome in this group – not only me, but my wife and my family – you can see why they’ve been so successful,” Allen said. “It’s such a great culture and great people. Footy aside, I’d do that 100 times over again.”

Advertisement

While Andrews, Berry and McKenna have been to the final week of the season on multiple occasions before, the experience is not entirely unique to Allen. “In my first year, in 2018, I was playing at West Coast when they won the flag. I was an emergency,” he said. Loading “So I went through the parade, going to Melbourne and all that. But to now be a part of it as a playing player is something I’m really looking forward to. ” Brisbane’s hunger has often been questioned this season, as commentators debated whether the Lions could repeat the feat of Leigh Matthews’ dynasty at the start of the century and chalk up a three-peat.

Advertisement

Allen and ruckman recruit Scott Draper have helped refuel the desire for success, according to Berry. “You can see how much it means to those boys,” he said. “At the end of the game, I think Drapes had tears in his eyes. Battered and bruised, Oscar Allen laps up the love of the Brisbane Lions faithful. via Getty Images “But there are also those guys who aren’t playing at the moment, you just want to do it for them – the hard luck stories.” No one should question the Lions’ appetite for victory this week, according to their skipper. It was on show during their third-quarter against the Hawks, reeling in a 14-point half-time deficit to take a 20-point lead into the final term.

Advertisement

“We saw in that third quarter how much we wanted it,” Andrews said. “We’re able to play – I don’t know what the score was in third – but play the right way and get the result on the scoreboard. “And then, in the end, we had to fight our way out of it. And we did.” Overjoyed Brisbane Lions fans welcome Harris Andrews into the change rooms after the win over Hawthorn. via Getty Images So, now, it is over to Fremantle. A side that has made one grand final in its history and never won a flag. They have the hunger, no doubt. But do they have the nerve against a hardened Lions outfit that can practically navigate grand final week in their sleep?

title: Jacques is worried his troupe will defect while performing in Brisbane. He’s only half joking
text:

NationalQueenslandEntertainment Jacques is worried his troupe will defect while performing in Brisbane. He’s only half joking Nick Dent September 20, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jacques Heim is a charismatic talker who uses your name for emphasis and delights in outrageous comments. He’s a natural showman, boyish for his 62 years, with the self-possession of a practised rule breaker. “Nick, I have to tell you, I was never a dancer, I was never a gymnast. I was never an acrobat,” he says in French-accented English. Escape is a spectacular production from Los Angeles playing Brisbane Festival. George Simian “I was a rebel, I was a punk, I got kicked out of six different schools in Paris. I was a little wild and so they had to put me in jail for a while, and then they let me go.

Advertisement

“So my family told me: ‘Jacques, you need to leave, you need to go to the land of opportunity, America.’ So I said ‘great’.” Heim is the founder and creative director of Diavolo: Architecture in Motion, a Los Angeles-based company bringing its daredevil style of performance to Australia for the Brisbane Festival. The company’s spectacular dance pieces involve huge geometric props that roll, pivot and swing while the performers climb, balance, hang, fall and jump. “This is something I will remember, it was incredible, congratulations,” Simon Cowell told the company after its debut on America’s Got Talent in 2017. (Diavolo would go on to be finalists.)

Advertisement

Surprise and delight are arguably in Heim’s blood: his grandfather and namesake was an influential couturier who shocked the postwar fashion world with his two-piece swimsuit the Atome – the forerunner of the bikini – and pioneered prêt-a-porter (ready to wear) clothing. “I guess some of my artistic juice came from him,” Heim says. “I’m really interested about what is innovation, how do you know if an idea is a good idea, how does it affect people?” Heim’s company performed in a routine with Dua Lipa at the 2024 Grammys. George Simian As the headline act for Brisbane Festival the company is presenting Escape, a show with 22 performers that “follows a group of humans as they … escape from their ordinary lives into a surreal landscape of infinite possibilities”. “The seed of the show started as revolting against the state of the world that we live in,” Heim says.

Advertisement

“You know what’s going on in the States. It’s a little crazy, especially with the government, who completely cancel every aspect of the arts.” (The Trump administration cut funding to the National Endowment for the Arts in 2025.) Related Article ★★★★

Entertainment Cirque in a grass skirt: Fijian Flying Circus gives aerial acrobatics a Pacific island twist “The reason it’s called Escape is very simply because we wanted to escape this crazy world that we live in, in the United States.” Heim does not need much encouragement to say what life is like in the country that has been his home for more than three decades. “When we were creating and rehearsing Escape, we had the ICE agents actually moving around our studio...

Advertisement

“I love America. I don’t want to be a hypocrite because it has given me so much opportunity, but I do have to say in a very genuine way: it’s not the same country.” Back in his punk days, in 1983, Heim attended liberal arts college Middlebury in Vermont, and started getting interested in acting. But his garbled English was holding him back, so when friends suggested he try dance instead something clicked. Performances skirt danger and are timed down to the millisecond. George Simian Architecture was another love, and he began to see parallels, formulating a style of prop-based movement that was not quite dance, not quite circus, and not quite acrobatics. Heim created Diavolo on graduating in dance from CalArts, and its first full-length show debuted in 1999.

Advertisement

By 2005, Heim was high profile enough to be invited to direct Cirque du Soleil’s show Kà, which is still running at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. “That was my PhD, because I learned a lot. I nearly got fired at least 34 times,” he quips. He is adamant that Diavolo is “not a circus company”. The distinction is a philosophical one: circus acts can involve danger, whereas danger, for Diavolo, is a “theme”. “I need to put my performers in a danger zone on purpose. Because when you put a group of people into a state of survival, they come closer together and help one another, they don’t think about themselves, but they think about others and how to create safety around each other. “So we have major safety protocols, and we have many steps that we implement.”

Advertisement

Pushing performers beyond their physical and emotional limits has been a feature of Heim’s performance workshops with military veterans, a program Diavolo launched in 2016 as a way of treating PTSD. Related Article Film & TV production Only heartstrings attached: Jim Henson and the evolving magic of puppetry “I operate as a drill sergeant. Even if some of the veterans are in a wheelchair, I ask them, can you get out of your wheelchair? Can you crawl? I make them crawl and move with all the dancers that elevate them.” Veterans have reported that taking part helped them avert self-harm. Heim received a Meritorious Civilian Service Medal for the program. He says his company is looking forward to performing in Brisbane for the first time, having previously appeared at the Arts Centre Melbourne in 2014.

Advertisement

“I hope my dancers will not defect and stay, because I have to tell you, Australia is a great country, has a lot of great arts. I won’t be surprised if some of my dancers decide to defect. “Who knows, Nick, maybe I will move the company to Australia, and I will never leave Brisbane?” I mention that the far right is on the rise in Australia too, and may have something to say about that. “Is it? It’s weird, because it’s happening in one country after the other ... No one is really safe today in 2026. “So how do we find equilibrium? How do we find a sense of hope? It’s about being together, it’s about creating a community. That was the core of Escape that we created among our 22 performers: a sense of community.

Advertisement

“At the end of the day, Nick, we’re from the same family called humans, and how can we support and help one another?” Escape runs at the Playhouse, QPAC, September 23-27.
